We examine the learning capacity of two-layer neural networks with respect to learning from the uniform distribution over a $d$-dimensional hypercube. Our approach involves approximating the neural network using a wide class of kernel machines, a method that yields an upper bound on the generalization error that degrades exponentially with increasing dimension $d$. For any fixed network, this finding establishes that its generalization performance is dimensionally stable. We also offer a matching lower bound, showing that the exponent in our upper bound cannot be improved. These results extend previous work by Dykstra et al. (2019), which addressed specific coordinate functions, to more general activation functions.

The UHECR anisotropy model, developed in collaboration with the Pierre Auger and Telescope Array observatories, is a two-component framework. Its first component utilizes a multipole expansion up to l=4, while the second addresses local fluctuations by drawing on the random walk hypothesis. Analyzing the latest data from both Pierre Auger and Telescope Array, our study reveals a growing dipole amplitude with rising energy, exceeding 4 EeV, and suggests that cosmic ray arrivals above this threshold are no longer completely random. Additionally, our analysis indicates a potential energy-dependent evolution in quadrupole amplitudes.

This paper investigates the homogenization of linear elasticity within sequences of increasingly thin layers. We adopt an energy approach, beginning with the derivation of formal limits under two specific configurations: layers with periodic structure and those possessing geometric almost-periodicity. These intermediate findings ultimately support distinct energy-based analyses, yielding rigorous energy-based convergence theorems regarding the geometric scenarios, as well as providing a microstructure-based analysis for the periodic case. The study further introduces an energy-based framework for a generalized operator of effective elasticity, as well as demonstrates a minimum principle applicable to the corresponding variational problems.

We demonstrate that for the semilinear wave equation defined on the Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) spacetime, every global solution exhibits superpolynomial growth relative to the timelike coordinate $t$ as $t \to \infty$, provided the future-directed timelike gradient of the spacetime is expanding and the equation's nonlinearity satisfies specific technical requirements. This result implies a polynomal lower bound on the non-supersuperpolynomial growth of global solutions under these conditions, thereby extending prior work by Baskakov, Kriegl, and Stehling (2021), who established only a linear lower bound for the same scenario in a maximally extended Minkowski space under maximal extendibility to the timelike direction.

Tumor Infiltrating Lymphocytes (TILs) are frequently assessed via microscopy of digitized tissue sections, a process heavily reliant on visual inspection by experienced pathologists whose subjective judgments can lead to inconsistent outcomes. This study introduces a deep learning framework designed to quantify TILs by analyzing images of cancer sections, with a specific focus on breast carcinoma. The model employs an attention mechanism to discern tissue boundaries and utilizes a dedicated detection head to identify TILs within the stromal interstitium. The system was evaluated on a dataset of 100 whole slide images (WSI) containing 1,000 manually annotated tissue areas. The results demonstrate that our approach achieves an average Dice coefficient of 0.81 and a mean absolute error of 0.13 when compared to expert annotations. These findings suggest that this method offers a superior alternative to manual assessment through its high measurement consistency, reliability, and reproducibility.

Cavity magnomechanics, an emerging discipline, utilizes the interaction between microwave photons in superconducting cavities and magnetic excitations within magnetic materials to enable precision sensing and robust quantum simulation. Although current experimental setups typically employ bulky three-dimensional components that hinder compactness and scalability, two (2D) magnetic materials present a promising solution by facilitating strong, tunable magnetocavity coupling through proximity effects. These materials also support rich magnon-phonon interactions essential for complex quantum control. In this study, we propose a scalable, tabletop quantum-stochastic model of a cavity magnomechanonic system based on a layer of magnetic materials. We analyze quantum-state engineering strategies to generate steady squeezed states and demonstrate that variability in system parameters allows for adaptable squeezing levels. Furthermore, we show that coupling magnons and phonons can significantly lower the variance of the squeezing depth achievable under fixed parameter constraints. Finally, we demonstrate the production of two-mode squeezed states and discuss the potential for applying this platform in quantum simulation and high-precision quantum sensing.

This research introduces a reinforcement learning (RL) framework designed for learning robust gaits that ensure stable locomotion for Cheetah quadrupedal robots. This method addresses three specific challenges: executing a "back-up" maneuver on a 3D slope, climbing a -motion while maintaining grip on a vertical, un-gripable surface, and climbing a motion while maintaining grip on a vertical, un-gripable surface. Hot winds are a prominent component of active galactic nuclei (AGN) feedback and are expected to influence galaxy evolution; however, the driving mechanisms and their efficacy remain debated. We utilized *Chandra* observations of nearby low-luminosity active galactic nuclei (LLAGNs) to examine the characteristics of these outflows. Our analysis indicates that the winds originate from hot, low-density cavities situated near the centers of the host galaxies. Specifically, the wind's terminal velocity is directly proportional to the ambient medium's density, demonstrating their thermodynamic origin. We propose that these jets inflate buoyant cavities which, as they rise, emit shockwaves that function as the driving force for the observed hot winds. This model offers a fresh perspective on how AGN feedback operates and its impact on galactic evolution.

Reinforcement learning offers a promising avenue for developing linear optimal regulators by leveraging state measurements alone, without requiring a system model. Nevertheless, standard off-policy learning techniques often suffer from slow convergence due to drifting away from stable system dynamics during the iterative update process. This work introduces a new design methodology for such regulators that operates without a system model and significantly accelerates transient learning rates. By employing a dual-system simulation technique, the approach keeps each learning step extremely small, ensuring rapid convergence while avoiding the need to re-run simulations from the outset at every iteration. Furthermore, under a mild technical assumption, it can be demonstrated theoretically that this method guarantees the stability of the system during the learning process.

The SiD Detector features an outstanding jet energy resolution, a feat achieved through a carefully balanced combination of an inner electromagnetic (ECAL) and outer hadronic (HCAL) calorimeter. Both ECAL and HCAL are constructed from high-granience, plastic-scintillator-tuned, hermetically sealed cells. This study presents the detector's simulation-based jet energy resolution and evaluates how variations in ECAL and HCAL cell sizes influence performance. Results indicate that the SiD detector's hadronic energy resolution surpasses standard predictions, while the jet energy resolution exceeds typical expectations for a general-purpose collider detector.

Deep learning has become a primary technique for addressing segmentation challenges in remote sensing imagery. To facilitate the evaluation of these methods and enable meaningful comparisons, this paper introduces EarthNets, a unified platform offering three distinct segmentation datasets: one for building footprints, one for land cover, and one for nightlights. Segmentation tasks remain highly relevant in remote sensing due to their extensive use cases and the numerous deep learning studies targeting them; however, these studies typically rely on scattered literature for benchmarking, which hinders effective performance comparison. Consequently, this paper presents EarthNets to standardize evaluations and simplify benchmarking through: (1) the provision of three high-quality remote sensing segmentation datasets, (2) the release of a unified codebase supporting state-of-the-art models across all datasets, (3) comprehensive experimental results, and (4) a rigorous performance analysis.

This study offers a theoretical analysis of large-scale behavior in two-dimensional active nematic hydrodynamics through a stochastic Landau-de Gennes framework. By solving these equations across various initial conditions and time scales, we observe that while long-range orientational order and the fluctuation-dissipation relation emerge at distances exceeding the correlation length, they break down in the short-range limit. Our results indicate that the system's behavior cannot be defined simply by an temperature; rather, a generalized thermodynamics emerges where a distinct, system-specific thermodynamic temperature governs the balance between active stresses and nematic elasticity.

Anomalies in chest X-ray images frequently appear as distinct region shifts in radiographic projections, often indicating critical medical conditions. While deep learning-based region partitioning methods have emerged to facilitate the detection of such anomalies, current grid-based partitioning schemes struggle with inaccurate boundary estimation, resulting in non-representative regions that fail to capture abnormal areas effectively. To overcome these limitations, this study introduces a novel dynamic region partitioning method. The methodology utilizes a trained deep learning model to generate anomaly heatmaps, which subsequently inform the creation of dynamic regions through boundary refinement. Specifically, a boundary adjustment network is employed to predict offset values relative to grid centers by analyzing heatmap data. These predicted offsets transform grid centroids into adjusted boundary positions. Furthermore, anomaly scores are calculated for each dynamic region by aggregating the localized heatmap intensities within the corresponding area. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed region partitioning technique significantly outperforms existing grid-based partitioning methods and several alternative regional deep learning approaches regarding abnormal region accuracy.

The discrepancy between experimental observations and Standard Theory predictions regarding the muon's anomalous magnetic moment is a significant issue. Recent work has highlighted a substantial role played by two-pion processes in this gap. This study examines how the two-hadron block influences the muon's spin dynamics by employing a model grounded in two-variable spectral functions, which are constrained by experimental data up to an energy threshold of 1 GeV. Our findings confirm that the two-hadron contribution is most significant in the lower energy spectrum (<1 GeV), amounting to approximately $-6.5 \times 10^{-8}$, a value that aligns closely with recent estimates derived using dispersion relations.

Recent advancements in large pre-trained models have significantly transformed programming tasks, specifically through their beneficial impact on downstream applications. Our comprehensive evaluation focuses on three areas: code completion, bug localization, and software vulnerability remediation, demonstrating how these tasks build upon one another. Specifically, we examine how incremental repairs in application layers can significantly enhance the performance of the code completion model, while our findings on how repairs aid bug localization surpass expectations. Additionally, pre-trained models demonstrate superior efficacy when utilizing repair contexts compared to when they only consider project or task-specific contexts. Our study reveals that bug remediation is particularly advantageous for downstream vulnerability repair and that the incremental repair process substantially boosts performance in these areas.

**Context:** The ongoing debate centers on whether the formation mechanisms of galactic discs and spheroids are distinct or unified. **Objective:** We aim to evaluate if current observations support a scenario where discs form in stable, gas-rich halos through coherent angular momentum acquisition, while spheroids develop in turbulent, rotationally unsupported environments. **Method:** We conducted a suite of cosmological $N$-body and gas-hydrodynamical simulations, utilizing both adaptive mesh and grid-based solvers, to simulate the formation of one or more spinners (disc-like galaxies) at redshifts $z=0$ and $1$. **Results:** We analyzed the dry and wet merger histories of simulated dark matter halos, alongside the rotation parameters of the resulting galaxies. **Conclusion:** Our findings indicate that the majority of single-spinner outcomes arise from mergers involving low specific angular momentum ($\lambda_{\rm \Delta}=0.03\text{--}0.06$) in halos of $10^{12}$ to $10^{13} M_\odot$. Furthermore, when comparing the outcomes of different numerical schemes, we observe that spheroid properties are consistently superior when employing 'zoom' techniques, whereas zoom simulations utilizing 'back-reaction' from gas dynamics yield spheroids that more closely resemble observed galaxies.

The all-sky all-sky photometric all-sky photometer (ASP) installed at the University of Wyoming provides a continuous, wide-field spectral snapshot of the sky every 10 minutes. This instrument measures the spectral irradiance of the sky across a broad range of wavelengths, enabling the derivation of the vertical aerosol optical depth ($\tau$) through the differential technique, which eliminates the need for absolute radiometric calibration. By applying a radiative transfer model to the ratios of spectral irradiances from adjacent channels, the differential method isolates $\tau$ while rendering results independent of variations in cloud cover, solar angle, surface reflectance, atmospheric absorption, and instrumental gain. Over the period from 2016 to 2020, this method yielded a daily $\tau$ value for each of the 12 spectral channels, which were subsequently averaged to generate a robust, calibration-free aerosol optical depth time series.

The Graphical Lasso framework is commonly employed to model an undirected Gaussian graphical network, yet it assumes all variables are observable. We propose a adapted Bayesian method that accommodates latent components within this framework. By introducing latent parts, our approach enhances variable selection accuracy and resolves ambiguities in edges between measurable variables caused by unobserved confounding. Using variational inference for scalable posterior approximation, we demonstrate the method's efficacy on both synthetic data and real-world datasets through numerical analysis.

We introduce a disk model designed to analyze the free-free and synchrotron components of the radiation from star-disk systems. In this framework, the electron temperature and density profiles throughout the disk depend on the ratio between viscous and viscous-plus-X-ray heating rates. We demonstrate that increasing an star's X-ray luminosity boosts the emission's free-free intensity and shifts its spectral peak toward lower frequencies. By examining specific disk configurations, we assess the applicability of classical single-temperature free-free models for data analysis. Our results reveal significant single-temperature assumptions can substantially underestimate the disk's synchrotron output and yield inaccurate estimates of key parameters, including the viscous timescale, surface density, and magnetic field strength.

This paper introduces a training strategy for autoencoders that enhances the performance of pitch autoencoders under noisy conditions. Current automatic pitch detection methods, which utilize autoencoders to isolate pitch-related speech characteristics from noise, face limitations due to clean-data training; consequently, background noise during inference distorts pitch values and generates spurious output. To address this, we propose a data augmentation technique that introduces random noise into the speech samples during training. This approach simplifies the augmentation process by directly employing noisy speech datasets such as the Noisy Speech Collection instead of requiring complex generation via noise synthesis and stochastic mixing. Our results demonstrate a significant reduction in the magnitude of erroneous pitch detections on both clean and noisy datasets, while also improving overall pitch estimation quality in real-world noisy environments.

In iterative methods applied to nonlinear equations, robustness refers to the capability to continue operating despite encountering non-convergent iterations, thereby preventing premature failure. While Anderson acceleration (AA) enhances the convergence rate of these methods, it lacks inherent robustness; however, regularization can be employed to regularize AA into a robust variant, termed regularized AA (R-AA). Building on this, Li et al. introduced the Data-Wrapper Anderson Acceleration with Out-of-Bounds (DWIFOB) algorithm in 2022, a method that enhances robustness by constructing a convex combination of historical data points to perform a line search for the optimal convergence parameter. This approach extends beyond the linear search limitations found in R-AA. This study investigates the robustness of the DWIFOB algorithm, demonstrating through numerical examples that it generally surpasses R-AA in robustness. Furthermore, we propose a new theoretical framework that unifies existing results on the robustness of both R-AA and DWIFOB, while also proving that the proposed characterization of DWIFOB's robustness properties is both necessary and sufficient.

We examine an extension of the Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (mSSM) comprising eight complex scalar fields and eight fermionic fields. Within our framework, we derive the conditions under which a light Higgs boson exists, demonstrating that the constraints imposed by a lightest Higgs boson are notably less restrictive than in the mSSM. Specifically, the prediction for this boson's mass can be enhanced, allowing it to exceed theoretical limits more easily due to the added neutrino fields. This mass elevation arises from the new interactions provided by the extended spectrum of particles.

Recent findings indicate that Neural Architecture Search (NAS) yields high-performance models that are often inefficient regarding training and inference, prompting a shift toward designing architectures for optimal efficiency without compromising accuracy. While some architectural elements like cell structures have been optimized for specific hardware, a comprehensive investigation into the program-level properties of efficient neural networks remains absent. We address this gap by analyzing a broad spectrum of neural architectures for both vision and language tasks, examining their structural and control-flow characteristics alongside performance and efficiency metrics. Our comprehensive study reveals that effective neural architectures consistently exhibit particular program properties, suggesting an underlying design principle for constructing such models. Furthermore, we validate these properties through controlled experiments, confirming their direct influence on both accuracy and efficiency.

Multicasting is a promising technique for enhancing the spectral efficiency of 5G wireless networks. However, transmitting a single data stream to multiple devices over disparate channels poses significant computational challenges, particularly within millimeter-wave (mmWave) systems. This paper introduces a low-complexity multiple-input–multiple-output (mmMIMO) multicasting framework designed specifically for 5G networks. We propose a joint multiple-beamforming and channel selection protocol that leverages the statistical correlation among channels to multiple users. By employing sequential testing to determine information gain, the traditional exhaustive search for precoder matrices is replaced with more efficient alternative rank-1 multiple beamforming solutions. Furthermore, we develop a novel multiple-peaks and channel selection algorithm based on sequential sampling using generalized likelihood ratio tests (GLRT). Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed frameworks substantially reduce computational complexity while simultaneously achieving performance metrics—specifically in terms of signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) and sum-rate—that closely mirror those of existing maximum likelihood methods.

This study introduces a new approach to reducing communication overhead in federated distillation by employing an innovative regularisation technique. We achieve this by adding a prior from a pre-trained encoder to the aggregated model at the server, which guides the clients in training their local models to replicate the representations of that aggregated output. Based on this mechanism, the proposed Compressed Federated Distillation enhances both the unique prior-induced regularisation and a quantization-specified prior to facilitate local compression. Notably, we demonstrate that this complete method improves its communication efficiency by a factor of two relative to standard Federated Distillation and doubles the efficiency of Federated Averaging while maintaining comparable accuracy. Additionally, we provide a theoretical proof showing that, under a linear probe setting, the representations produced by our method converge to those of the pre-trained encoder, thereby regularising the final model.

Service discovery and orchestration are essential for automating end-to-end (E2E) delivery in cloud environments. Traditional methods often struggle with scalability and effectively balancing load. This paper introduces Service Discovery Assisted Dynamic Orchestration (SDADO), an algorithm designed to enhance E2E delivery by optimizing delivery paths through intelligent service discovery and dynamic orchestration strategies. Testing within a Kubernetes-based cloud simulation demonstrated that SDADO significantly outperforms current leading algorithms regarding throughput and end-to-end delay. Specifically, SDAO achieved approximately 30% higher throughput and reduced E2E delays by nearly half. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that service discovery based on the "most complete" approach yields better delivery performance than methods relying on "most specific" or "most popular" strategies.

We investigate the exponential stability of an interlinked mass-spring arrangement within a star-shaped metric graph featuring $n$ edges, where only the first edge has a spring-loaded slope while the remaining $n-1$ are frictionless. This specific configuration, distinguishing itself from prior studies of mass-spring networks on graphs, addresses a scenario that had not been previously analyzed. By applying Bessel functions and Laplace transform methodologies, we derive an explicit formula for the mass-spring system's spectrum and establish a necessary and adequate criterion for exponential stability. Finally, we demonstrate that this arrangement remains exponentially stable regardless of the parameters governing the spring on the elastic edge.

We have established the spectrum of chiral fluctuations associated with the chiral condensate $\langle\bar qq\rangle$ in the presence of quarks and gluons within an inhomogeneous matter environment. Our analysis reveals that instability arises exclusively through instability in the pseudoscalar sector, ultimately resulting in chiral symmetry breaking. To achieve this, we first constructed the effective potential governing the order parameter $\langle\bar qq\rangle$ as a functional of temperature $T$, chemical potential $\mu$, and wavelength $1/R$, utilizing the one-loop thermal approximation alongside an anfangian that explicitly incorporates back-reaction from the condensate. Our findings, computed on an one-loop level including this mutual back-reaction, are subsequently contrasted with earlier second-order $\delta$-function approximations and mean-field models that treat $\langle\bar qq\rangle$ as a screening background field.

An agent equipped with a utility function can optimize any task by maximizing that function's value. While prior research largely focuses on the agent acquiring this function online through comparative feedback, we investigate an offline setting utilizing expert knowledge. We observe that utility functions derived solely from the relative preferences of outcomes often fail to align with those inferred from professional judgments, even when those preferences come from within specific domains. Consequently, we introduce a new class of parametric functions designed to better capture the nuance found in expert assessments. We further develop an alternating optimization algorithm to learn these functions from historical result rankings provided by experts within various contexts. Through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, we demonstrate that functions trained exclusively offline from the tendency of expert knowledge to differ from pure outcome comparisons, and that an online learning approach is frequently necessary when available.

This paper presents a study on forecasting future actions for agents trained via Reinforcement Learning using Sequence-to-Sequence models. We investigate how STMs can predict an agent's subsequent movements by analyzing existing data, exploring this approach through various scenarios. Additionally, we evaluate the STM approach alongside a Long Short Term Memory (LSTM) model against a Markov Chain baseline for comparison.

We introduce a framework for modifying properties within the zero-temperature zero-energy Hamiltonian of a cold-atom system situated on a lattice. Utilizing Weyl's perturbation theorem of finite rank, we show that by superimposing distinct perturbation Hamiltonians that commute with the original operator, one can adjust a system's band structure. Specifically, these methods allow the strategic creation of Weyl nodes and their manipulation into loops or surfaces of constant zero-energy momentum, a capability demonstrated explicitly in the creation of such loops or surfaces in the context of zero-energy band structures under cold-atom conditions.

In risk-sensitive reinforcement learning (RL), the objective is to maximize the expected utility of the total discounted reward, where utility depends on a specified risk aversion parameter. For finite Markov decision processes (MDPs), a risk aversion parameter that is too large can lead to exponentially difficult problems, motivating the use of algorithms that leverage "exponential tilting" to L. This paper demonstrates the efficacy of incorporating exponential tilting into standard algorithms used to solve linear programs (LPs) for solving the risk-sensitive MDP via minimax duality. Specifically, we prove theoretically and show practically that integrating a "restart" strategy with an existing risk-sensitive MDP solver based on linear programming significantly enhances its effectiveness.

The growing prevalence of public project data on version control platforms and issue trackers presents valuable opportunities for data-driven research into development processes. However, the vast scale and heterogeneous formats of these datasets often restrict analysis to small samples, preventing generalizable conclusions. This study addresses four research questions regarding public Jira projects—focusing on issue activity patterns, interactions between Jira and GitHub data, correlations between project maturity metrics and issue activity, and comparisons across industry verticals. To facilitate these investigations, the authors present a comprehensive, pre-processed dataset comprising 522MB of compressed data (1.1GB uncompressed) that integrates issue histories and comments from 388 days of Jira logs with linked GitHub repository source code and commit logs for 935 public projects. This collection represents the largest available dataset of connected public Jira and GitHub records to date. Due to the substantial volume and diverse modalities of the data, the authors employ distributed data analytics techniques, specifically leveraging Apache Spark for processing and Keras for modeling. They also introduce a customized Hadoop file system format designed to maintain data integrity across nodes during processing. Access to the dataset and accompanying documentation is available at https://github.com/ResearchITMS/Dataset-Jira-Issues-Comments-Linked-To-Commit-History.

Federated Learning (FL) represents a pivotal approach in privacy-preserving machine learning, enabling clients to train global models locally without transmitting sensitive raw data to a central server. This study introduces Weighted Power-T Mean (WPM), a novel aggregation function for FL that offers greater flexibility compared to standard methods like server average or weighted average. By integrating WPM as the aggregation layer, we develop a new algorithm capable of converging to a stationary point of the global objective function, with the degree of convergence controllable via an adjustable power-T parameter. Our experimental results across image classification and sentiment analysis tasks demonstrate that WPM-enh FL algorithms outperform both linear aggregation baselines and traditional linear aggregation schemes in terms of accuracy.

We introduce an optoelectronic device designed to generate and read out the quantum state of isolated atoms that have been trapped using far-off-resonance optical tweezers. By integrating a single atom with a microwave cavity through a tweezers-coupled electric dipole, we achieve efficient state preparation and detection for hyperfine levels. This architecture holds significant promise for technology such as single-atoms cavity quantum electrodynamics (Cavity QED) quantum memory and the development of scalable atoms-for-clocks networks.

This study introduces a novel class of discrete models for percolation defined on valuated oriented graphs. Specifically, we percolate a countable random model consisting of percolated graphs equipped with non-negative edges weights. A key finding demonstrates that for a broad category of these graphs—specifically those formed as quotients of zigzags—the tails of the resulting critical distribution share a common limit regardless of the chosen graph within this class. Additionally, we establish a continuity property concerning both edges and Eienstein bond weights within these valuated graphs by examining their limit behavior.

We introduce a new method for inferring polymers that employs a novel data-driven variational inference approach. Unlike traditional techniques limited to inferring only the nearest chemical unit or a fixed window of monomers, our algorithm characterizes a polymer as a sequence of its constituent monomers weighted by specific emission probabilities. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through simulations based on the 1-D Ising model and through an analysis of real-world audio transcription data.

Although a medical facility may have multiple single ventilators, each dedicated to one patient, a shared ventilator system allows several patients to be supported by one device while maintaining the specific tidal volume and airway pressure requirements for each. This paper introduces a switching control strategy designed to meet these constraints by treating the system as a system of linear differential equations with time-dependent coefficients. We establish the strict positiveness of air pressure and tidal volume under certain conditions on time-dependent parameters, demonstrating simultaneously that each ventilator generates the precise tidal volume requested by its respective patient. Furthermore, this approach provides two additional advantages: it reduces equipment costs and eliminates the need to calibrate pressure sensors for every individual ventilator.

This paper investigates the template for the dynamics of rational functions $z \mapsto z^{d}R(|z|^{2})$ where $d \geq 2$ and $R$ is a rational function with two critical points. Initially, we characterize all possible subgroups of deck transformations arising from the iterations of these bicritical rational maps. Subsequently, we construct a countable collection of countable groups that equipments with group operations to form valid template dynamos for the iterations of such maps.

This study examines a class of Bayesian regression models incorporating sparsity priors over the regression coefficients, with the unknown error variance treated as a separate parameter. By analyzing these models under the framework of a complete model including variance uncertainty, we assess posterior contraction rates relative to the true parameter values. Our approach begins with the standard assumption of a proper prior for the inverse gamma distribution used on error variance. Under this condition, and assuming the complete model satisfies standard identifiability, consistency, and entropy conditions, we demonstrate that posterior contraction rates for the complete model match those achieved when variance is known. Specifically, with squared-error loss functions, the contraction rate for the variance parameter itself is determined to be $n^{-1/2}$. However, for coefficient parameters estimated via squared-error loss, the contraction rate degrades by a factor of $\log^{1/2}(p/n)$ compared to the scenario where variance is assumed known, reflecting the additional uncertainty introduced by the unknown variance. Extending this analysis to alternative loss functions, such as 0-1 or squared-Huber loss, which incur greater penalty on large errors, results in slower posterior contraction rates for both the variance and coefficient parameters when variance uncertainty is considered. These findings highlight the critical impact of variance uncertainty on estimation precision, particularly in settings involving large numbers of predictors.

This paper examines the impact of machining parameters on surface roughness, a critical quality metric, utilizing a full factorial design of experiments. Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) was employed to determine the significance of individual factors and their interactions regarding surface roughness. Results indicate that Depth of Cut exerts the most significant influence, accounting for 53.88% of surface roughness's total variability, followed by Feed Rate at 33.81%, with the interaction between these two parameters contributing an additional 10.16%. Using the Signal-to-noise ratio within Taguchi's methodology, optimal settings were identified to minimize surface roughness. Subsequently, a regression model was developed and validated, yielding a high coefficient of determination (R²) of 0.9667.

We investigate the mixing between two mesons characterized by their natural parameters, specifically the mixing angle. By analyzing various experimental observations involving decays and production mechanisms, we derive constraints on hadronic properties, including the mixing angle itself, which we term the "mixing angle parameters." Our analysis reveals two distinct, widely separated regions in the allowed parameter space that align well with existing data. By examining the theoretical underpinnings of this two-region structure, we gain enhanced understanding of the dynamics. Furthermore, within the second region of the allowed parameters, we investigate potential $g$-parity violating interactions, ultimately arguing against their presence based on both theoretical considerations and experimental evidence.

Digital signatures are increasingly integral to secure data exchange across various sectors. Consequently, the ability to authentically verify a signer's identity is critical for ensuring received data's integrity. Although handwritten signatures offer low creation costs and high convenience, their extensive and frequent usage can compromise their secrecy. To mitigate these risks, ensuring a signature's integrity demands robust forgery detection systems capable of identifying counterfeit signatures. This study investigates the influence of a user's specific signature template distinctiveness, complexity, and repeatability on the efficacy of such systems. Through an analysis comprising 1,200 signatures drawn from 40 individuals, the research examines how detection algorithms perform across 10 different templates, each augmented by 10 generated fake signatures. Empirical results indicate that the accuracy of current state-of-the-art algorithms varies significantly depending on the inherent distinctiveness, complexity, and consistency of specific signature templates, a factor often disregarded in existing literature.

We perform an analysis of how supersymmetry constraints affect the specific forms of low-energy effective couplings within D String theory. Our results indicate that the $D_5$-branes act as sources for a rank-5 tensor, while $H_5$-dual sources are attributed to $D_5$-branes; in this context, the five-form potential is absent in $D$ String theory. We further examine supersymmetry constraints alongside gauge anomalies to assess the viability of these predictions.

We investigate the influence of thermal fluctuations on $n$-point correlation functions for a general lattice many-body quantum system at finite temperature. For a system with a quadratic dispersion relation, we derive an upper limit for $n$ points beyond which all connected correlation functions vanish due to the free-space nature of the theory. By employing a momentum-space expansion applicable to arbitrary interacting or non-interacting three-dimensional lattices, we demonstrate that for any Lennard-Jones or bcc interacting or non-interacting models, thermal effects suppress long-range order of spinless bosons in contrast to what occurs in one or two dimensions. Additionally, we show that similar connected correlation functions exhibit significant suppression near the nucleation points of charged matter within U(1) Schwinger models in three dimensions.

We introduce a novel approach to studying galactic chemical evolution by utilizing a data-driven method to model element correlations. Using observational datasets from the Milky Way's halo and the globular cluster system M13, we apply machine learning techniques to derive the following findings: a) The [N/O] ratio rises quadratically with [O/H] as a function of metallicity, yet remains constant over cosmic time; b) Alpha-element correlations with iron mirror established latitudinal gradients, showing higher ratios in both the Milky Way and M13 for lower metallicities, with a distinct separation between the two systems; c) Oxygen abundances in M13 exhibit a stronger correlation with iron compared to the Milky Way, and the peak [O/H] in M13 is significantly lower than that of the Milky Way. Additionally, our results indicate that a one-zone chemical model incorporating secondary nitrogen production can successfully reproduce the [N/Fe] trends in both systems. These findings suggest that a simple secondary model for nitrogen adequately explains the trends in both the Milky Way and M13, with the latter's evolution potentially resulting from early supernova feedback that halted star formation.

Research in Natural Language Processing (NLP) has seen exponential growth in recent years, driven by vast corpora and powerful computational capabilities. While this field traditionally focused on English, recent strides have enabled the development of multimal systems capable of handling over 1,000 languages. These advancements have opened new research avenues, addressing limitations faced by low-resource languages and presenting significant opportunities for developing inclusive multilingual systems. Given that over 8,000 people globally rely on these under-supported languages, there is an urgent need to ensure access to cutting-edge NLP technologies for these communities. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of current NLP capabilities across diverse languages, examines ongoing efforts to broaden system support, and offers a detailed examination of emerging application domains. By doing so, it aims to equip researchers with an overview of the landscape and identify promising future research directions to foster progress in these less-resourced areas.

Advancements in networked data and graph theory have proven essential for understanding complex biological systems, such as gene regulatory networks, brain dynamics, and ecological interactions, by offering a framework to model these systems and their associated diseases. This paper specifically examines the 1D and 2D spatial layouts of such networks, demonstrating that the robustness of their topological structures can be effectively characterized through the solvability of the Positive Definite Kernel (PDK) problem and the derivation of their Graph Signaling Algebra (GSA). Furthermore, the study investigates how the attributes of their one-dimensional projections relate to the fundamental order properties of the resulting spatial arrangements.

This study examines a self-conjugate bi-doublet scalar extension within the Left-Right Symmetric Model (SR-Sym) in light of recent white dwarf (WD) observational data. We demonstrate that WD measurements impose constraints on the model's parameter space derived from a combination of radiative and gravitational influences on WD structure. Specifically, these constraints are derived by evaluating the single-to-double energy correction alongside the scalar contribution to osmotic pressure. Our analysis indicates a strong correlation between the parameters limiting the physical region defined by Higgs mechanism effects and those governing the scalar osmotic pressure. When these observational limits are cross-referenced with existing limits from collider experiments, dark matter searches, and proton decay searches, we determine that the parameter space compatible with all constraints allows for potentially testable predictions regarding signatures at future high-energy colliders.

Recent studies have attempted to safeguard images within visual classifiers by either obscuring class labels or removing private attributes through prior research. Building on these efforts, our study shifts the privacy removal process from graph node labels to the images themselves while maintaining the image-based graph structure. We introduce the Graph Privacy Advisor, a framework offering flexible control over how deeply private information is stripped from both the graphs and the associated nodes. By evaluating removal strategies across various degree distributions and removal probabilities, our experiments demonstrate that the Graph Privacy Advisor consistently surpasses existing models in classification accuracy while effectively lowering private classification accuracy (PCA) to ensure true proprietary status remains ambiguous. Furthermore, we developed an optimal strategy for graphs generated by our proposed distribution model, which significantly boosts performance in the Graph Privacy Advisor compared to alternative approaches.

This paper examines how statistical entanglement influences entropy flow within various radiation models. The study reveals that, contrary to expectations, entanglement does influence the radiation's entropy evolution. The paper derives a closed-form formula for the entropy current's divergence, which functions as the right-hand side of the Reynolds transport equation applicable to this statistical framework. The model demonstrates how to account for the entropy current's influence on the total entropy change within a moving volume, which includes contributions from an extensive source term. The analysis indicates that contributions from this entanglement-related term are significant and cannot be disregarded. The study finds that, contrary to earlier beliefs that such effects are negligible, they are substantial. The entanglement-related source term constitutes a significant factor in radiation dynamics, and the proposed closed-form solution provides a rigorous analytical framework for understanding the entropy current's divergence in this specific statistical context, confirming that such effects are far from ignorable. This study details a measurement of transverse momentum ($p_{\perp}$) spectra for jets and their constituent partons within central lead-lead (Pb+Pb) collisions at a nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}} = 2.76\ \mathrm{TeV}$. Jet and hadron yields were measured with associated photon triggers to probe the sequential modifications occurring within the quark-gluon plasma. The findings indicate that, when normalized to the photon $p_{\perp}$, both jets and constituent partons exhibit similar suppression trends in the high-$p_{\perp}$ regime ($\gtrsim 20\ \mathrm{GeV}$), whereas hadrons show distinct behavior. Furthermore, jet and parton spectra display significant shifts compared to those of untagged jets; specifically, they exhibit less suppression at low $p_{\perp}$ and greater suppression at high $p_{\perp}$. These observations suggest that central high-energy Pb+Pb collisions induce distinct energy-dependent and species-specific modifications to jets and constituent partons in the context of the quark-gluon plasma.

This article reviews recent and emerging computational methods for solving the time-dependent Schrödinger equation (TDSE) that exploit low-precision (8 to 16 bits) arithmetic. These approaches are highly parallel and scalable, making them ideal for integration with future specialized low-precision hardware. By natively leveraging this hardware, the methods tap into significantly higher floating-point operations per second (flops/s) and a substantially expanded memory footprint. The text begins by briefly outlining current high-accuracy, high-cost techniques—specifically spectral methods and the Split-Operator Spectral Method (SOS)—used for TDSE solution. It then introduces novel, cost-effective strategies, including the Spectral-Grid Method of Lines (SGM), the Adaptive Phase-Grid Method (APG), and the Adaptive Phase-Space Method (APS), along with a comparative analysis of their performance. The discussion concludes by examining how these low-precision native methods scale across both traditional and emerging specialized hardware architectures.

The foxsi balloon-borne instrument has conducted a series of solar observations, including the first series focused on the quiet Sun. These campaigns captured X-ray images of the quiet solar disk and its corona for the first time, revealing no detectable disk emission in the imaged coronal regions. Detecting such faint signals is technically demanding; however, foxsi's ability to track the moving sun and its high-speed on/off cycling makes this first observation possible. This paper details foxsi's tracking performance, presents the resulting data, and offers a comparison with other solar X-ray instruments.

This paper examines influence prediction within social networks, addressing the challenge of limited labeled data in graph-structured environments. We introduce TAA-GSP, a novel framework that combines train-and test-time data augmentation with the PageRank algorithm for influence prediction. Our approach leverages multiple data-augmented versions of the original graph to compute weighted PageRank scores, effectively incorporating augmented graph information while original graph data serves as the baseline. We evaluated this method on real-world social graphs of varying sizes, comparing results against a baseline using the native graph alone as well as various augmentation techniques. The study specifically investigates how different strategies for calculating these weights—such as uniform, baseline, and squared influence influence—affect model performance. Our findings indicate that for smaller graphs, test-time augmentation significantly boosts accuracy, whereas larger graphs see minimal gains. Furthermore, we observe that the superiority of our weighted-augmentation approach over the baseline primarily depends on the influence distribution across the network, with uniform weighting yielding the most consistent performance improvements.

Optimizing specific functional forms within quantum field theory often proves challenging, yet this approach has become a widely used technique for determining functional spacetimes. We demonstrate that associated Euler-Arnold equations can transform an inherently intricate optimization problem into a more tractable system of nonlinear equations. Furthermore, our findings indicate that applying the Euler-Arnold flow toward certain functional ansatz types can accelerate convergence through periodic trajectories. Ultimately, our method offers a novel mathematical framework that can be extended to analogous optimization challenges in other domains.

This work addresses sensor fusion in pose estimation when incorporating noisy relative pose measurements derived from featureless contexts, such as camera hand-eye calibration for robots or vehicle navigation. Unlike traditional methods that rely on linear relationships or independent error assumptions, our approach models complex, non-linear error correlations. By accessing raw data and incorporating more generic correlations, the algorithm achieves higher precision in estimating the relative pose between any two sensors. Although designed within a hand-eye calibration framework, this approach extends to general multi-robot or vehicle navigation scenarios involving featureless estimation. We introduce a variational Bayesian extended Kalman filter (VBEKF) capable of adapting to varying levels of effort in capturing error correlations, allowing a trade-off between computational cost and estimation accuracy. Furthermore, the proposed method remains robust against non-Gian noise distributions and non-linear dependencies.

This study explores cosmological constraints on dark matter by applying a "multi-temperature universe" framework, which allows the dark matter interaction cross-section to vary across scales. Within this model, we explore parameter spaces capable of addressing the $4\sigma$ excess in XENON1T data alongside other cosmological and experimental limits, including CMB, Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN), direct detection results, and indirect detection measurements. Our results indicate that a contact interaction between nucleons and dark matter fermions can explain the XENON1T anomaly if the coupling is strong at short distances ($\sim$1 fm), approximately $10^{-3}$ fm², while remaining compatible with BBN constraints. Furthermore, the predicted excess in cosmic ray antiprotons from this scenario is found to be consistent with current experimental uncertainties.

This study reports on a search for standard model same-sign W boson pairs ($WW$) at ATLAS using 139 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data recorded at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV between 2015 and 2016. The analysis targets a final state comprising two leptons (electrons or muons) of the same electric sign, two jets, and missing transverse momentum. The event selection strategy employs two distinct topological categories: one featuring two jets tagged with b-quarks in the same event, and another with none. An initial data significance of 4.1 standard deviations indicates a clear excess, primarily aligning with the anticipated standard model $WW$ signal. Under the hypothesis of no signal, a standard model-only fit yields an observed significance of 4.1$\sigma$, with an expected significance of 2.9$^{+0.4}_{-0.3}$(stat)$^{+0.5}_{-0.4}$(syst). Furthermore, measurements of fiducial cross-sections were derived, showing data consistency with standard model predictions. Additionally, limits on anomalous WW coupling and the production cross-sections of heavy charged vector bosons were established.

Although recent colorization methods have significantly advanced, many are rigidly constrained by an ineffective fixed set of colors, limiting their universal application. We introduce a novel, trainable color palette that can adapt to various domains, effectively addressing this limitation. Our method employs a palette containing just 100 colors represented in LAB space, which is initialized with a sampling from LAB-space uniform distribution and subsequently refined by maximizing the log-likelihood of training data. Capable of generating high-quality colorization across diverse domains using a single universal palette, our approach also facilitates direct comparison against currently available methods. Comprehensive evaluations on three image datasets and extensive experiments with various paints underscore the superior performance and flexibility of our solution.

The $P(q)$ model serves as an alternative to Lambda Cold Dark Matter, specifically designed to address the Hubble tension. In collaborative coding ecosystems like GitHub, shared files serve as vital communication channels for conveying design and functional details. This study examines the maintenance practices of such files across three distinct repository types: open-source projects, proprietary software, and educational settings. Our analysis indicates that while shared files are maintained with greater care in these diverse environments, the specific strategies employed vary significantly. We further explore the implications of these findings on collaborative coding workflows and document maintenance.

We conducted a comprehensive spectroscopic and photometric study of the binary system BD And, located in the southern hemisphere. Our findings indicate that BD And is a close, semi-detached Algae variable consisting of an early F-type primary star and a low-mass secondary companion. Analysis of the system's orbital light curve and spectroscopic data yielded an orbital period of 0.428880 ± 0.000002 days, along with precise inclination (80.8°) and mass estimates of 1.15 M$_\odot$ and 0.16 M$_\odot$ for the primary and secondary stars, respectively. Rotational velocities were determined to be approximately 30 km s$^{-1}$ and 50 km s$^{-1}$ for each companion. While previous investigations classified this system as an eclipsing polar, our data reveal that the polar characteristics stem from the primary star itself. Furthermore, examination of the out-of-eclipse spectral regions suggests the presence of an additional third component, likely a low-mass M-type star, which is hypothesized to be responsible for the previously reported H$\alpha$ emission features.

To enhance the accuracy of aspect-based recommendations, this study introduces a novel User Preference Learning framework called ABL-GATE. At its core lies the Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module, designed to simultaneously capture long-term user behaviors and refine aspects-related preferences within user embeddings. Specifically, a dedicated long-term aspect preference layer is implemented to model coarse-grained user aspects, while time-sensitive interactions are modeled to refine these coarse preferences based on recent activities. Additionally, a dual-layer attention mechanism is employed to emphasize significant recent interactions, which then modulate the user aspect embeddings through both series and parallel gating structures to construct the final refined aspect embeddings. These enhanced representations not only improve overall recommendation precision but also provide interpretable insights into recommendation reasons. Extensive experiments conducted on two real-world datasets confirm that ABL-GATE substantially outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, with the GAPE module's dual-path gating mechanism showing distinct advantages in modeling diverse user behaviors and fine-tuning aspect preferences for the task.

This study explores the obstruction theory concerning symplectic sheaves, $\mathcal{S}$, defined on a sheaf of homological dimensions equal to 1. Through this theoretical examination, we establish that, given a specific resolution of such a sheaf consisting of smooth spaces, the obstruction classes are explicitly realized within the corresponding first-degree hypercohomology.

We apply the principles of $q$-calculus, specifically utilizing generating functions with $q$ as a parameter to investigate partitions subject to restrictions on part multiplicities. This approach offers a streamlined method for deriving generating functions and systematically presenting identities regarding isobaric polynomials and their reciprocal variants. Moreover, our method provides sufficient conditions to generate functional equations that facilitate the derivation of numerous partition identities.

We analyze the weighted least squares algorithm for computing the optimal projection of a given function onto a subspace spanning a set of basis functions using exact basis evaluations sampled with noise. Our framework adopts measure-theoretic perspectives, establishing the connection between subspace spanned random features and high-dimensional statistical components. We further establish the connection between our approach and Gaussian process regression through the lens of Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces. Based on these insights, we demonstrate the stability of weight least squares and prove optimality theorems regarding the scheme for various families of feature functions. Our approach yields explicit error bounds for general scenarios and provides detailed optimization rates for functions exhibiting polynomial growth.

The hadronic model for the near-threshold X(3872) particle's formation is re-examined using a more rigorous treatment of its internal structure. This approach influences model parameters by defining them through a specific functional form of the Hiegler-Lee-Polchinski mechanism's wave function, specifically an exponential decay for the binding potential. This proposed structure serves as a critical input to the Gazal's initial conditions for the reaction, directly impacting the calculated phase-space rates. The study analyzes how variations in the wave function's shape affect the generated rates and investigates the sensitivity of the model to initial state assumptions by altering the density profile at X(3872)'s formation point. These findings offer new insights into the particle's formation dynamics and suggest constraints on X(3872)'s physical properties that can be tested against LHCb experimental data.

The local moment interactions observed in disordered semiconductors like Si:P originate from the Coulomb force between an implanted donor's localized electron and its surrounding hole wavefunction valence band. To investigate this, we employ a tight-binding model that incorporates both electron-phonon coupling and electron-electron Coulomb forces. In this study, we calculate the g-factor and zero-field hyperfine coupling for isolated local moments, offering insights into the interaction mechanisms between bound excitons and local spins. Our calculations reveal that the local spins' hyperfine interactions with 12 nearest-neighbor valence bands are predominantly mediated by Coulomb forces with holes localized on the same nearest-neighbor sites as the donor bound excitons.

This research investigates the impact of symmetry breaking on the non-perturbative conservation laws regarding scalar field theories with $O(N)$ symmetry and their associated axial $U(1)$ current. While conservation laws hold in the perturbative framework, they are violated at the non-perturbative level due to singularities that prevent the cancellation of commutators involving the axial current divergence and time evolution generators. The study demonstrates that utilizing explicitly symmetry-broken symmetry-preserving (SP) potential formulations yields distinct conservation behavior at the non-perturbative level, with several such potentials analyzed.

This paper presents a methodology for robot acquisition of real-world skills in complex, unknown environments. The core challenge lies in distinguishing between confounding factors that affect task success, as these vary depending on the specific elements of a chaotic environment. To achieve this, we employ a hierarchical Bayesian model that infers the root causes of confusion by referencing a library of physical laws and their outcomes. By isolating these defusing factors, the method enables the effective transfer of learned skills across diverse settings. Our approach utilizes a probabilistic causal graphical model to represent the relationships among task components, incorporating directed acyclic graphs to formalize the hierarchy of these factors and support efficient inference. Furthermore, we integrate causal interventionist do-operators to emulate active learning strategies, allowing the robot to deliberately query the environment to identify defusing variables. We validate this framework through a case study involving a mobile manipulator tasked with pushing an object through a cluttered landscape.

The topological study of the whisker and lassol topology on classifying spaces and related algebraic structures has been extensively documented. In this paper, we establish several novel findings concerning these topologies on the space $\tilde{X}_H$. Specifically, we prove that for any topological group $G$, the whisker and lassol topologies agree on $\tilde{X}_H$ precisely when $K(H,1)$ is finitely presentable as a group. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a quotient map $f: \tilde{X}_H \to X$ preserves completeness and is a homeomorphism under the respective topologies applied to $\tilde{X}_H$ and $X$, again if and only if $K(H,1)$ possesses finite presentation.

Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has proven effective for high-dimensional control challenges, yet its application to high-dimensional planning—such as robot arm navigation or autonomous driving—remains limited. This paper introduces a novel DRL framework for motion planning, formulated as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP). To overcome the prohibitive computational costs associated with solving such POMDPs, we propose a new policy gradient algorithm that mitigates the need for vast data sets by restricting exploration to a motion trajectory generated from a specific initial state. Empirical results demonstrate that our method significantly surpasses traditional search-based approaches in cost-efficiency and matches traditional methods in sample complexity.

We have developed a novel method to simulate galaxy evolution, incorporating gas accretion onto central black holes (BHs) that follows an Eddington-type limit. Unlike standard models, this approach establishes a direct proportionality between the central BH's mass and the galaxy's stellar mass, as the Eddington limit scales with the central mass-to-light ratio. By adopting a simple "box" model for star formation, we find that this runaway Eddington accretion naturally accounts for the observed $M_{\bullet}-\sigma$ relation. Furthermore, this mechanism drives starburst episodes that supply fresh fuel for further accretion, offering a potential explanation for quasar variability. In our numerical experiments, we discovered that this feedback-regulated accretion generates substantial star formation, contributing significantly to a black hole mass fraction of up to 30% of the total galactic black hole mass over a typical star-forming period. Additionally, the resulting star formation episodes may provide the episodic energy releases attributed to AGN variability.

Recent advancements in ensemble-based deep learning uncertainty quantification (UQ) demonstrate that prediction confidence estimates from such methods are reliably calibrated. Leveraging these well-predicated confidence metrics, we present a new deep learning model reclassification technique designed to improve outcomes by automatically targeting specific tasks. Although traditional deep learning reclassification approaches exist, they often demand extensive manual expert review to identify misclassified samples. In contrast, our proposed ensemble ensemble method (hereafter referred to as "CER") offers a fully automated mechanism for reprocessing prediction samples. By ranking sample reprocessing based on the likelihood of correction using confidence-derived metrics, we highlight the superior performance of our method on a variety of datasets across classification tasks.

This study investigates the advantages of open access preprints by examining 1,000 mathematics papers to benchmark how these documents influence publication velocity, citation counts, and the dissemination of findings. The analysis compares preprint versions against a control group of similar works where the authors did not utilize preprints. Results indicate that preprints significantly accelerate the publication process and substantially boost an article's citations relative to non-preprint counterparts. Furthermore, the findings suggest that preprints foster more effective knowledge dissemination, even in the field of mathematics, which historically has been characterized by limited sharing of draft materials.

This paper introduces an integrated, automated system designed to connect laboratory instrumentation with electronic documentation. By mapping instrument data points directly to specific sections in paper notebooks and electronic records, the system uses tailored scripts to gather results and populate the appropriate documentation fields while preserving links to raw data. The implementation involved wirelessly networked spectrophotometers and a microplate reader communicating with both traditional handwritten notes and digital records within a university-based undergraduate biology course. By eliminating manual transcription, this solution significantly reduced the incidence of human error in sample identification and data entry. Course instructors monitored the impact of this tool on student collaboration, learning outcomes, and the overall efficiency of experimental workflows and resource use.

Recently, machine learning has emerged as a pivotal tool for predicting complex materials phenomena, including phase formations, microstructural evolution, and mechanical responses. While applications in ceramics and ceramics-based composites are growing, this field has received significantly less attention than its counterpart in metal alloys. This review explores the use of data-driven and physics-informed machine learning models for materials science, with a primary focus on ceramics and ceramics-based composites. We examine various machine learning applications, including phase formation prediction, mechanical properties forecasting, and microstructural analysis. Furthermore, we examine the principles, advantages, and limitations of both approaches, while assessing the current state of ceramics-related datasets and identifying future opportunities within this rapidly evolving domain.

The two-charm tetraquark $T_{cc}^{+}$, discovered in 2022, decays via the two-body channel $T_{cc}^{+}\rightarrow D^{*+}D_{s0}^{*}$. This study examines final state interactions (FSI) involving $D D_{s0}^{*}$ and $D_{s0}^{* 2}$ pairs in this decay. Employing the boson form of the Weinberg equation combined with the framework of the hadronic molecular model, we calculate the corresponding hadron form factors. Our analysis indicates that $D D_{s0}^{*}$ contributions significantly outweigh those arising purely from $D_{s0}^{* 2}$ interactions.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) have emerged as a highly effective framework for machine learning tasks that can be expressed as subspace learning. In subspace learning, data points are projected into a cluster-specific subspace to facilitate classification; this process relies on constructing a graph where a graph convolution operation serves as the projection mechanism. This study introduces a theoretical connection between popular GNN operations and subspace learning by analyzing how established graph operations—such as those representing connectivity, random walks, and independent component analysis—define the resulting graph matrix properties. We demonstrate that certain graph convolutions project data based on graph independent components, thereby providing a new theoretical basis for understanding how GNNs achieve effective subspace learning.

Recent findings establish that for the finite projective plane over the field $\mathbb{F}_q$, complete Sidon sets are currently known only when embedded within one of the two conic sections, or fit inside a specific union of lines. Building on this, our work investigates the completeness of Sidon sets within the finite affine plane $\text{AGL}_2(q)$ by drawing parallels between them and those in the projective setting $\text{PG}_2(q)$. While this analogy allows us to extend certain construction techniques—yielding lower bounds for maximum sizes of complete Sidon sets in affine configurations—we also identify crucial differences between the two contexts. Ultimately, our analysis suggests it is likely impossible for a Sidon set in the affine plane to be contained in a full projective line. These considerations collectively offer a pathway toward resolving the completeness problem for Sidon sets within both the finite affine and projective planes.

This study addresses the challenge of sampling binary matrices with a fixed row sum configuration and a column sum configuration that is unknown. We propose an efficient algorithm that generates matrices according to a non-uniform probability distribution, offering a framework for analyzing binary matrix models. This approach holds significant potential for applications in fields such as neuroscience and ecology. We demonstrate the model's capabilities through numerical results, comparing the properties of matrices produced via our non-uniform sampling method against those from uniform sampling.

Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) serves as the fundamental theory describing the strong interactions of quarks and gluons. While the DGLAP equation governs how parton distribution functions (PDFs) evolve with scaling variables, these functions are theoretically defined only within this specific evolution framework. Consequently, every PDF set must be characterized by an input scale ($Q_0$) and adhere to specific boundary conditions at $Q_0$, which are determined by global fitting procedures against experimental data. These fits operate under specific theoretical assumptions, such as the particle spin assignments for input distributions. This paper presents a novel, flexible framework utilizing a state-space model to perform a joint fit of PDFs and DGLAP evolution parameters directly from data. This approach enables the simultaneous extraction of PDFs and evolution parameters specific to the fitted scale $Q_0$, free constraints from PDF sets designed for lower scales. Furthermore, it allows for the assessment of correlations between the evolved parameters and the input distributions, as well as the investigation of how PDFs and DGLAP parameters respond to datasets with varying degrees of theoretical dependence on the distribution shapes.

This article details the technical evolution of our software package, specifically focusing on the period from 2015 to 2019. It outlines how these advancements enhanced performance and scalability, ensuring a smoother integration with modern web-based environments. We achieve these results by employing domain-specific techniques alongside general data mining strategies. As this work offers an extensive overview of our technical advancements, it serves as an excellent primer for researchers and developers interested in system-level optimization within data mining.

This study introduces a novel technique for generating sidebands in microcombs using sideband pumping of a microresonator. By adjusting the spacing between sidebands and demonstrating that the microcomb's spectral response responds to such spacing, the method proves versatile for producing complex optical comb patterns. The study shows spacing dependence experimentally by demonstrating a sideband separation of 25 GHz and showing how the microcomb's spectrum responds to such changes, the method proves useful for engineering light with intricate comb spacings. The method experimentally verifies spacing dependence with, for example, 25 GHz between sidebands, the method proves helpful for engineering light with intricate comb spacings.
