This study presents the results from SEM-TAB-FACTS, a shared semantic evaluation of tables and text entailment. The assessment involved eight participating groups working across three subtasks. Task 1 requires classifying the relationship between a table and an accompanying natural language sentence into one of three categories: entailment, contradiction, or neutral. Tasks 2 and 3 focus on extracting specific information; Task 2 asks for the identification of all supported, contradicted, or neither claims regarding various natural language queries derived from the tables, while Task 3 entails listing every supporting fact or pointing out all incorrect sentences relative to a given textual input and table data. A total of twenty-two dataset sets were provided for training and testing purposes. The evaluation gathered 104 submission attempts across the three tasks, resulting in 92 successful submissions: 45 for Task 1, 31 for Task 2, and 15 for Task 3. No participant successfully completed Tasks 2 or 3 more than once. The analysis details the data construction process, reports individual and collective participant performance, and evaluates various performance factors. The findings indicate that pre-trained semantic models combined with 2D convolutional neural networks offer strong results for Task 1, whereas both tasks benefit significantly from integrating2D and 3D spatial convolutional architectures to handle the complex extraction requirements of Tasks 2 and 3. The complete code and model weights for the top-performing teams will be released

The formalism of quantum mechanics relies fundamentally on complex numbers; however, some researchers have attempted to fathom the theory through real numbers only. These efforts typically involve recasting existing equations in real terms, yet they fail to illuminate the reasoning behind original physicists' choice to utilize complex numbers. These narrations merely rephrase real-formulated axioms to assert that complex versions hold equally valid. In contrast, these authors propose a reconstruction where a real-number base theory uakes logical room for the introduction of complex numbers. By building quantum mechanics from this real foundation, the author aims to reveal why complex numbers are inherently necessary within the framework of quantum mechanics.

The metric dimension of a graph refers to the smallest possible cardinality of a resolving set. Truncating distances within an unweighted graph involves removing all edges between vertices at a graph distance exceeding a specified threshold $k$. We demonstrate that for paths and for trees excluding a fixed subtree, this truncation operation becomes "phase-transition-like": once the parameter $k$ surpasses a specific value, the resulting metric dimension abruptly shifts from small to large and remains so, exceeding the dimension of any graph obtained with greater distance parameters.

This study examines the one-dimensional steady-state flow equation for a leaky aquifer exhibiting spatially changing conductivity. Although analytical solutions exist for the specific case where hydraulic conductivity changes linearly with depth, this work derives a solution applicable to any functional variation of conductivity using numerical methods based on finite differences. The resulting approach simplifies the steady-state flow equation, enabling its resolution via

This study investigates the impact of reactor dimensions on the elimination of $SO_x$ in an O₃-UV system through numerical simulations of the inhomogeneous-k model within a 3D framework. The model incorporates the mechanisms of $NO_x$ and $SO_x$ formation, the destruction of ozone, the generation of reactive species, and subsequent reactions leading to sulfur dioxide removal. Three distinct reactor configurations were simulated to analyze how reactor size, specifically volume or mass, and residence time influence the extent of $SO_x$ removal. The results indicate a strong correlation between the degree of $SO_x$ removal and $NO_x$ formation in O₃-UV reactors. Furthermore, there exists a relationship linking reactor volume or mass to the required residence time for achieving complete $SO_x$ removal. Additionally, reactor mass influences the peak concentration of generated $NO_x$; larger reactors produce higher maximum $NO_x$ levels compared to smaller systems.

This study introduces a novel, accelerator-centric framework designed to assess and contrast neuromorphic architectures for embedded systems. Focusing on the impact of various virtual platform configurations on both design complexity and simulation velocity, the work presents a comprehensive comparison of three configuration methods applied to RISC-V-based neuro-morphic platforms. Configured using three distinct approaches—manual setup, automated generation via the OYVAIN platform, and controlled exploration through the Kaspar multi-core framework—these platforms were simulated under diverse workloads. Key metrics such as co-simulator overhead and specific computational tasks were analyzed to reveal significant performance disparities. The findings indicate that while current simulation speeds may lag behind real-time requirements, the selection of virtual platform architecture critically influences simulation efficiency, with the OYVAIN-generated virtual machine demonstrating the highest speedup ratio compared to other tested configurations.

The inference stage is critical in machine learning, as it involves applying trained models to new data to generate predictions. While inference is typically prioritized for its ease of execution, existing approaches often overlook specific efforts to enhance this phase. This paper introduces Indecision Trees (IDT), a novel class of classifiers designed to deliberately optimize the inference step. By representing the inference stage as a constrained Markov Decision Process (MDP), Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) IDTs dynamically select an appropriate expert for each prediction based on input features. Evaluating these classifiers on various benchmark datasets demonstrates that they rival standard high-performance classifiers in accuracy. Furthermore, the study reveals significant potential for speeding up expert inference within MoE IDTs, validating the approach's effectiveness.

We introduce an innovative technique for performing fast similarity searches in time series data that combines two key components: (i) an Index of Tree structures optimized for low memory usage and (ii) Access mechanism accelerated by early termination. While current Hierarchical Clustering based Index (HCI) methods rely on pre-computed cluster access to prune the search space, our approach goes further by supporting early abandoning based on real-time distance lower-bounds during neighbor traversal, a capability previously unattainable with standard alternatives like ivIndex or SIFT. Empirical results demonstrate that our early abandoning strategy, paired with the hierarchical index, significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art ivIndex in both accuracy and speed.

This study evaluates the efficacy of automated feedback provided by a compiler interpreter in a first-year Java course. Participants were divided into three groups receiving either no feedback, line-level feedback, or project-level feedback. Results indicated that compared to the control group, both types of feedback significantly enhanced code coverage and improved programming scores on the second, third, and fourth assessments. Nevertheless, the project-level feedback group achieved higher average scores on the second exam but scored lower on the third exam relative to the line-level group. These findings underscore the value of immediate post-submission automated feedback in introductory programming contexts, highlighting a critical consideration for instructors in selecting between line or project focus.

Sympolitic surrogate models have emerged as an effective approach to interpreting black-box classifiers by constructing simplified, understandable approximations of their decision-making processes. The core strategy involves solving an optimization task to determine the parameters of a simple model that minimizes discrepancy from the target classifier's outputs. Although black-box attacks are inherently noisy due to experimental constraints, existing techniques lack robust methods to account for this noise. This paper presents a novel attack framework capable of launching note-routant attacks while explicitly handling noise. Our attack leverages the output probabilities generated by the target classifier rather than discrete labels, integrating these probabilistic estimates directly into the observables of the model recovery process. Experiments conducted on various classifiers within both tabular and real-world text domains demonstrate that our method significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques in scenarios involving noise.

Over-smoothing represents a critical limitation in Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), causing them to converge prematurely on identical node representations and degrading performance. This study investigates the temporal evolution of these over-smoothing dynamics, revealing inherent algorithm-specific properties that vary with network architecture. Furthermore, we demonstrate that while standard GCNs are susceptible to this issue due to an inherent implicit bias toward it, adding dropout can serve as an effective strategy for preventing over-smoothing. These insights provide a foundational framework for researching algorithms capable of accurate graph learning even after the over-smoothing process has initiated.

This work examines simplified framework models for describing dark matter interactions with quarks and leptons. We analyze two distinct scenarios: (i) neutral, spin-1/2 dark matter produced via vector, scalar, or pseudoscalar mediators, and (ii) neutral, spin-0 dark matter produced through vector mediators. For each framework, we compile comprehensive tables detailing the cross-section formulas and Lagrangian structures, organized by production mechanism and mediator type. Additionally, we outline the corresponding effective field theory frameworks and present limiting cases where specific results converge to effective field theory descriptions.

This study introduces and analyzes the theoretical framework for spin-dependent parton correlation functions, featuring one additional longitudinal spin index relative to standard correlations. The extra index corresponds to the transverse motion of partons within hadrons. Correspondingly, we demonstrate that these new functions enable the construction of dihadrons with spin $J=2$ from quark-antiquark pairs, thereby allowing access to the parton's transverse momentum dependence structure.

The Categorical Summation Property (CSP) applies to any metric compactum that maintains this property even when combined with products involving the Closed Long Ray ($\overline{R}$) or the Long Line ($\mathbb{R}_l$). CSP itself signifies that for any compact metric space $X$, all homeomorphisms within the group $\text{Homeo}_c(X)$ featuring compact support are dense within $\text{Homeo}(X)$, considered with the compact-open topology. Additionally, a metric compactum $X$ exhibits CSP under specific conditions if it possesses a universal subset $U$ (a 2P-space) within some metric compactum. This article demonstrates that both CSP and its dual property (DCSP) extend to a wide variety of classical spaces, notably including $\overline{\mathbb{R}}_l$, $\mathbb{R}_l$, the Hilbert Cube, the Hilbert Space, and the product $\overline{\mathbb{R}}_l \times \mathbb{R}_l$.

The synthesis of hexagonal domain HgTe on graphene substrates via chemical vapor deposition is achieved at growth temperatures of 350 °C or higher, whereas lower temperatures (below 350 °C) result in the formation of cubic domain HgTe. Transmission electron microscopy and X-ray diffraction analyses indicate that the hexagonal phase possesses superior crystalline quality. Furthermore, transport measurements demonstrate that Hall mobility in hexagonal domain HgTe exceeds 10 cm²/V·s, a significant improvement over the mobility observed in the cubic domain material.

This study examines the estimator $\hat{r}_n$ for the number of common stochastic trends in $n$ time series, which functions as the smallest integer satisfying the conditions of cointegration and stochastic trends. While estimating this parameter is typically straightforward with limited evidence supporting its robustness, this paper investigates $\hat{r}_n$ under the challenging scenario where data exhibit heavy tails. By employing classical $L_2$-based spectral Gramian matrices and establishing their behavior under multivariate domain of attraction conditions for multilinear arrays with multilinear weights, we analyze $\hat{r}_n$. Our findings demonstrate that $\hat{r}_n$ remains consistent across various scenarios involving heavy tails and varying sample sizes. Additionally, we provide an extensive empirical evaluation demonstrating $\hat{r}_n$'s consistency and reliability even when data deviate from standard Gaussian assumptions and feature significant kurtosis.

We conducted a weak lensing analysis of the massive galaxy cluster MACS J0717.5+3741, revealing that its south-western subcluster exhibits a complex pattern of small-scale distortions. We demonstrate that this structure cannot be accounted for by the smooth gravitational potential of substructure alone; rather, the observations indicate the presence of numerous lenses with masses approximately $10^{9} M_{\odot}$, likely corresponding to perturbers in the range of $10^{9}-10^{10} M_{\odot}$. These objects may represent small satellite clusters or a population of galaxy-sized objects, though current data preclude definitive mass determination or identification of their specific nature. While such perturbers are known to impact large-scale cluster properties like mass and concentration, their influence on substructure weak-lensing reconstructions remains uncertain. We illustrate that in certain scenarios, these small-scale features can significantly alter the fine details of the lensing convergence map, particularly in regions of high magnification. Consequently, we argue that future weak lensing studies must explicitly model the effects of unseen perturbers to avoid misinterpreting residual small-scale noise as evidence for additional cluster substructure.

This study examines a content delivery network (CDN) framework in which a content provider (CP) contracts with multiple internet service providers (ISPs) to distribute web traffic. CP's goal is to contract with a subset of these providers, directing effort levels accordingly, while each ISP independently decides its own investment based on anticipated requests, which it perceives as the total effort from all content delivery efforts divided by its own share of the contract. We analyze two scenarios: one where all ISPs possess private knowledge regarding their investment costs, and another with publicly known costs. First, we establish the existence, uniqueness, and properties of the Nash equilibrium within the ISP layer for the private cost scenario. Next, we derive a Stackelberg equilibrium, where the CP acts as the leader by optimally partitioning the market among the ISPs. Our numerical experiments compare the total benefits of the content delivery system under both a cooperative alliance of the ISPs and non-cooperative individual decisions. Results indicate that ISP cooperation leads to higher investment efforts and significantly greater payoffs for the content provider compared to the non-cooperative setting. Furthermore, we derive a closed-form lower bound for the CP's maximum profit resulting from optimal cooperation.

This paper demonstrates that any arbitrary category can be embedded as a full subcategory within a weak 1-categorical framework. In this alternative context, standard notions of functoriality, universal properties, and adjunctions acquire modified definitions—specifically, they become "weakly" formulated. Despite these adjustments, all canonical constructions from the purely categorical approach remain valid when expressed in this weakened setting. Moreover, we establish that embedding arbitrary categories into this weak categorical domain can be achieved via a unique (up to isomorphism) universal property that mirrors the behavior already observed for weak cartesian closed categories and weak homotopical categories.

We examine $ eta$-attractor models featuring both exponential and polynomial forms within the no-scale framework, assessing their compatibility with cosmological data through the reduced chi-squared statistic ($ eta$-reduced$) for comparison. Our findings indicate that exponential $ eta$-attractors consistently demonstrate a superior fit to cosmological data across all tested scenarios with $D$ data points and parameters $ eta$. We further establish a minimum threshold of $ eta$ required for compatibility with observational evidence and evaluate potential detectability of deviations from the attractor behavior by future experiments, specifically those succeeding Planck. Additionally, we explore the relationship between this approach and existing literature on no-scale superpotential modifications in supergravity that emulate $ eta$-attractor properties.

A measured bending lamination within a quasi-Fuchsian manifold corresponds to a unique conformal structure on the boundary of the universal cover; however, this handholding property fails in all neighborhoods of the Fuchsian locus. The demonstrated result is that every such bending lamination can be realized as a combination of simple closed geodesics found on a manifold exhibiting an eight-shaped glue pattern of conformal structures. Furthermore, the study addresses the related question of the non-uniqueness of manifolds in these eight-shaped configurations.

We establish the moments of the log-normal distribution describing the time-series distribution of capital returns, generated by the constant growth duration gamblers ruin model where investors gradually shift a portfolio from a high-risk asset into a risk-free asset. Within this framework, the initial four moments of the resulting cross-sectional returns distribution correspond directly to the moments of the individual asset returns. Furthermore, these theoretical findings align closely with empirical data drawn from actual financial markets.

Detecting cardiac abnormalities is vital for timely diagnosis and effective treatment planning. Although deep learning has advanced this field using noisy electrocardiogram data, it often relies on noisy, pre-labeled datasets that are costly and difficult to source. This study introduces a novel self-supervised learning method designed to enable effective training on completely unlabeled ECG data. By employing a contrastive learning framework, we create two augmented views of the input through concatenation with its time-reversed counterpart and apply temporal shifting. Our time-reived model demonstrates superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Additionally, we developed a novel synthetic dataset featuring diverse notches and spikes to better reflect variability found in clinical scenarios.

This study employs the Multi-Configuration Self-Consistent Field (MCSCF) method to calculate the $ns2p\ ^{2}P^{\circ} - ns2s\ ^{2}S$ transition in $\mathrm{Be}^{+}$ ions, a process unmeasured experimentally. We decompose the resulting electric dipole amplitude into distinct components arising from Configuration Interaction (CI), the E1 operator itself, and the E1 electron repulsion (ER) interactions, labeling these as Main, Core, and Tail contributions respectively. Specifically, the CI and Tail terms represent amplitude changes due to configuration mixing on the Hartree-Fock (HF) level, while the Core term denotes the E1-only contribution. Notably, the CI and Tail parts are mutually independent of E1. Our analysis of relativistic MCSCF results using both Douglas-Kroll-Hess (DKH) and Dirac-Hartree-Fock (DHF) HF references reveals that all three contributions are necessary for precise dipole moment determination.

We offer a novel, explicit formulation of equivariant cohomology $H_{\mathbb{Z}}^*(\mathbb{T}^n; \mathbb{R})$ for the cases where a finite group $G$ acts on the torus $\mathbb{T}^n$ via a discrete subgroup of $GL(n, \mathbb{T})$. This description offers a geometrically intuitive framework that clarifies the role of twists in equivariant cohomology. A corresponding framework is also proposed for twisted group cohomology $H^*(G; \mathbb{R})$.

I argue that an improved internal climate directly correlates with better research outcomes. To achieve this, I will explore the significance of both community and collaboration, as I believe both are essential for fostering a positive departmental environment. I will also examine the role leadership plays in cultivating such a climate, as well as the necessity of addressing systemic issues like bias and inequity. Ultimately, I will outline strategies for individuals to proactively enhance the department's atmosphere.

This study establishes the boundedness and non-boundedness properties of the fractional series operator $T_\alpha$ defined on the toral setting. Specifically, for parameters $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and $1 < p, q < \infty$, the operator is defined by $\widehat{T_\alpha f}(n)=\frac{\widehat{f}(n)}{(1+|n|)^{\alpha}}$. We demonstrate that if $\alpha \leq 0$ or $\alpha > \alpha_0(p,q)$—where $\alpha_0(p,q)$ is a specific constant—the operator $T_\alpha$ fails to be bounded from $H^p(\mathbb{T})$ into $H^q(\mathbb{T})$. Furthermore, for parameter ranges $0 < \alpha \leq \alpha_0(p,q)$, we provide precise endpoint estimates that bound the operator norm $\|T_\alpha\|_{\mathcal{L}(p,q)}$. In doing so, we show that this study completes the complete characterization of boundedness for fractional series operators on the torus.

This research investigates the strategic behavior of sellers in environments where buyers possess private valuations and may engage in break rules, specifically by submitting bids exceeding their true valuations. Sellers aim to maximize revenue by incentivizing compliance through a second-price sealed-bid format; however, our findings reveal that even when non-credibility prevents this optimal design, sellers significantly increase revenue by establishing and enforcing penalties for bidding more than one's true value. Because complete rule adherence by buyers rarely occurs in the absence of such sanctions, a broken auction design does not necessarily preclude revenue maximization. Our analysis provides a specific parameter set where sellers achieve the highest possible revenue by breaking non-credible incentive schemes that impose penalties, a strategy that supersedes the alternative of a broken non-punitive rule or no rule at all. Furthermore, we establish that these three potential outcomes—the choice between a broken rule with punishment, a broken rule without it, or implementing neither—are mutually exclusive for any given environment.

This study investigates anisotropic cosmological models featuring a plane-symmetric electromagnetic field representing the early universe. The researchers demonstrate that while anisotropy is inherent in the initial epochs, the model naturally evolves toward isotropy as the universe ages. Additionally, a representative numerical analysis is provided to illustrate how plane-symmetric electromagnetic and fluid components influence the anisotropy of the universe during its formation.

We investigate the unipotent Hessenberg varieties associated with unipotent elements in the Lie algebra of a Borel subgroup of a simple algebraic group over a field of characteristic zero. For the case where the Hessenberg function is linear, we derive explicit equations for these varieties and apply combinatorial techniques to analyze how their local generators interact. By utilizing the established connection between the Gaudin model and Lie algebra cohomology, we apply second-generation Poincaré-Birkhoff-Witt theorems to establish the second generation Poincaré basis in the algebra. This framework enables us to apply Lie algebra methods effectively within the algebra, using the resulting Lie algebra relations to determine the Gr\"obner bases of the local defining ideals. Consequently, we can explicitly describe the coordinate rings of the corresponding Hessenberg varieties.

The recent surge in AI-generated artwork has captivated both artists and the general public. While current literature extensively documents applications of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) in art, this work investigates their specific utility in creating AI-assisted painting assistance. We propose utilizing GANs to produce stylistic brushstrokes that can fill designated areas according to a user's input stroke. We initially outline a method that GANs can synthesize new imagery by blending attributes extracted from multiple reference images. Following this, a technique is demonstrated where the network locally warps a specific source image to conform to the geometry of a hand-drawn sketch. Finally, we explore using the GAN to generate texture details that fill regions defined by this warped image.

Recent flavor anomalies observed in the $P^{0}S^{0}$ and $P^{0}E^{0}$ decays of $B$-mesons have sparked significant interest, particularly given the potential violation of lepton-flavor universality. This study examines the branching fractions and ratios for these decay modes within the framework of QCD factorization, utilizing predictions from LC sum rules. Our analysis reveals consistent patterns across the $P^{0}S^{0}$ system, where we find that ratios between different lepton flavors align well with standard QCD factorization expectations and LC sum rule pre-calculations. Furthermore, analogous behaviors are observed in the $P^{0}E^{0}$ sector. By comparing our numerical results with experimental data from the Belle collaboration, we obtain consistency across both models and the standard QCD factorization approach for these specific decay channels.

**Title:** Natural Language Question Answering Using the Non-Controling Dataset: New Dataset and Model.

**Abstract:** Natural Language Question Answering (NLQA) involves generating responses to inquiries posed in natural language, representing both a pivotal and highly difficult area within Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Computational Linguistics (CL). This paper introduces a new dataset and advanced model designed to enhance the accuracy of NLQA systems by leveraging the power of Large Language Models (LLMs). This new dataset, called Non-Controling Dataset (NCD), is built from a new non-controller language construction method. NCD is a large-scale, high-quality corpus containing over 10 million questions and their corresponding answers in natural language, covering a wide range of topics and difficulty levels. This new dataset is developed to address several limitations of existing datasets, including their small size, limited topic coverage, and lack of difficulty diversity. This paper also presents a new multi-task learning approach for improving the accuracy of NLQA systems using NCD. This approach leverages the power of LLMs to enhance the accuracy of NLQA systems by training them on NCD. This approach has demonstrated significant improvements in the accuracy of NLQA systems using NCD, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin. This paper concludes by discussing the potential future applications of NCD and the multi-task learning approach for enhancing NLQA systems.

We have conducted a comprehensive study on the evolution of rotational core collapse in both successful and failed supernovae, covering all stages from initial infall through post-shock stagnation to the final black hole formation. Extending our previous work, we now analyze the dynamics of the convective, global non-axisymmetric (m=1) and magnetorotational (m=1) wobbles that arise immediately behind the shock in non-rotating, spherically symmetric progenitors with magnetic fields. Unlike prior studies that assumed the wobbles were already present at birth, we demonstrate that these instabilities can be triggered by the stalled supernova itself. Our findings indicate that in non-rotating progenitors, both the m=1 and magnetorotational instabilities invariably cause the supernova to either explode or black hole-form significantly earlier than they would without such triggers. Furthermore, we found that the development of these wobbles is more rapid in the presence of a magnetic field. Consequently, black hole formation occurs sooner, producing a broader distribution of final black hole masses dependent on the initial progenitor mass and strength of the magnetic field. These results suggest that the black hole mass distribution serves as a diagnostic tool for understanding the role of magnetic fields in core-collapse supernovae.

Although Deep Learning models utilizing Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have demonstrated strong performance in classifying Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) through functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) data, they typically depend on computationally expensive processes to identify regions of interest (ROIs) and extract features. This reliance on complete data processing limits their suitability for scenarios involving data scarcity or the need for rapid analysis. Consequently, this study introduces a modified Deep Learning approach that trains on only the subset of highly relevant ROIs, significantly reducing both computational load and the amount of data required. Specifically, we employed a modified DenseNet-121 with a reduced depth of 18 layers, integrated with a ResNet-18 structure to enhance feature learning efficiency. Our results indicate that this architecture achieves an accuracy of 70.46% using just 20 critical ROIs, a marked improvement over a baseline accuracy of 58.33% obtained using the standard, unmodified DenseNet-121 on the full dataset.

Finding fixed points is a fundamental challenge in mathematical modeling. For a broad class of non-linear operators defined within a specific function space, we establish that an interior fixed point, when it exists, must be unique. Consequently, for these operators, a data dependence result applies. It is worth noting that although these operators generally lack a solution boundary fixed point, they frequently do have one. Under certain conditions, we demonstrate that a boundary fixed point, if it exists initially, can be transformed into an interior fixed point. Based on this, we prove that for a subclass of these operators, an interior solution is the only possible solution. Finally, we examine these theoretical findings in relation to a boundary value problem for a non-linear, degenerate, viscous, conservative system of equations representing two-dimensional axial symmetry for an incompressible, viscous fluid.

Acronyms play a vital role in communication by conveying specific meanings through shortened forms. Although acronyms are often introduced with their full definitions, these explanations are frequently omitted in practice. This absence of definition complicates understanding, particularly for readers encountering the abbreviated term for the first time across diverse writing domains. To address this challenge, developing systems capable of predicting a term's defined meaning from surrounding contextual clues is essential. In this study, we present new neural network-based models designed to identify and disambiguate acronyms from text. Specifically, our training data is derived from 22 million acronyms gathered via Wikipedia infoboxes, and our approach is validated across three distinct domains using held-out test sets.

Heat transport within quantum Hall systems has been a focal point of theoretical research for over twenty years. While heat conformation relies on inter-edge scattering to occur, heat *rectification* can be realized through inter-edge *thermal* localization. This inter-edge thermal localization results from the interplay between the chiral nature of edge motion and the specific coupling mechanisms connecting edge channels. We offer an extensive analysis of rectification in both quantum Hall ferromagnets and antiferromagnets. Specifically for quantum Hall ferromagnets, rectification arises from either asymmetric spin-precession frequencies or asymmetric coupling between the two spin modes of the edge. In contrast, within quantum Hall antiferromagnets, the rectification mechanism involves competing precession frequencies alongside asymmetric coupling.

Data storage using DNA presents a potentially data-intensive solution, yet current approaches often lack the scalability needed for practical, large-scale deployment. This paper introduces a new framework for organizing DNA data storage partitions that leverages the library structures of existing literature. By utilizing primers as partition identifiers, our method automatically generates unique IDs for each section, eliminating the need for costly experimental validation of identifier uniqueness. Furthermore, we developed a secondary method for locating and removing specific partitions through targeted PCR, offering a mechanism to manage data compaction on the same hardware as the storage process. The effectiveness of our proposed partitioning system and the results from various removal experiments using laboratory-grown *E. coli* are detailed in this study.

Beyond standard non-Hermitian topological polarization characterized by a real non-zero value, we reveal the existence of topological nodal lines within the momentum domain of Hermitian systems. These lines are defined by nodal points that exhibit a finite dispersion, a trait resulting from the presence of PT-symmetry breaking. We introduce a topological invariant to identify the winding number of these lines and provide determinant formulas for calculating the winding number of the corresponding momentum-space nodal lines for generic models. It should be noted, however, that these lines lack protection; they can be closed or eliminated by minor perturbations. Furthermore, we reveal an interplay between these lines and topological polarization, revealing that the latter can induce the former. In conclusion, we reveal an interplay between these lines and topological polarization, showing how the former can induce the latter. We reveal a strong connection between the two, where topological polarization can induce the formation of these lines in nodal lines, demonstrating their shared topological nature.

Imaging biobanks are collections of paired medical images and corresponding clinical annotations that serve as valuable resources for assessing, developing, and implementing artificial intelligence models in healthcare. The rapid expansion of these biobanks presents critical design and execution challenges, primarily concerning data privacy, governance, and interoperability. This article outlines current best practices for establishing and managing imaging biobanks, emphasizing regulatory compliance, standards, and best practices to ensure alignment with regulatory requirements and operational effectiveness. Furthermore, we highlight emerging opportunities and potential solutions that may shape the future of these biobanks.

This study examines the role of data augmentation in predicting COVID-19 severity using Electronic Health Records (EHR). We assess various techniques, including those leveraging clinical features and similarity between patient records, alongside synthetic EHR generation. Our findings reveal that similar to other healthcare tasks, these methods yield limited performance when EHR are scarce and clinical features are unavailable. However, we observe significant improvements in similar learning scenarios when clinical features exist. Specifically, similar-to-cov learning and synthetic data generation surpass similar-to-cov learning when applied to similar, cov cases. We also note that such similar, cov methods are particularly advantageous when used alongside clinical features and demonstrate greater resilience to data scarcity in comparable cases, such as cov. Our codebase is accessible at https://github.com/your-repository-link (please replace with your specific url).
An introduction to the theory of polymatroidal ideals, along with examples drawn from problems related polynomial ring structures and polymatroidal complexes, follows.

K-means clustering is a fundamental unsupervised learning technique widely used for grouping data points based on their proximity to cluster centers. While numerous quantum algorithms have been suggested for this purpose, they typically rely on quantum random sampling to achieve an asymptotic complexity of $O(N)$, representing a significant reduction from the $O(N^2)$ requirement of many classical approaches. This study introduces a quantum algorithm that leverages quantum phase estimation to determine distances between data points and cluster centers utilizing the period-finding technique. By applying binary quantum phase estimation, the proposed method utilizes fewer qubits and achieves a lower computational cost of $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{N})$, marking further advancements beyond existing methods.

We report the discovery of 11 planetary events in the K2 mission's first phase using the standard transit method. This application reveals a previously unidentified class of events, demonstrating that the direct imaging of exoplanets is feasible even when the companion is significantly less massive than its host star. Our findings provide the initial observational constraints on the mass-ratio function for planet-planet pairs, suggesting a uniform distribution between $10^{-3}$ and $10^{-1}$. Based on the current event count, we project that the standard method will eventually identify approximately 300 planetary systems, primarily within the mass range of $10^{-3}$ to $10^{-1}$.

Accurately simulating shadows is essential for creating realistic scenes in computer graphics. Conventional techniques, such as ray tracing, are typically employed for this purpose, but these methods can be computationally expensive. This paper introduces a method that improves both accuracy and real-time performance by approximating shadow computation through the utilization of ray tracing results during the sampling of directional lights within a voxelized scene. This approach renders the computation of shadow functions significantly more efficient. We achieve this by partitioning the scene into voxels and pre-calculating the number of rays that intersect each voxel once at the beginning. During the main rendering phase, the algorithm approximates the blocked light volume by multiplying the precomputed voxel data by the voxel span. Finally, this approximation is used to estimate the number of occluded rays by a subject, thereby accurately and efficiently simuting shadows in real time.

Probabilistic Origin-Destination (O-D) demand modeling relies on estimating an $N \times N$ covariance matrix derived from $N$ origin-destination pairs, a task that is computationally demanding. Furthermore, real-world data often suffers from scarcity, resulting in poorly estimated covariance matrices. This study addresses these challenges by applying Lasso regularization techniques to enhance estimation accuracy. Although Lasso produces a sparse matrix that aligns well with the structurally undefined nature of O-D demand, its performance relies on converting the continuous covariance matrix into discrete demand values, thereby introducing a potential approximation. To mitigate this, the authors propose an iterative approach that alternates between estimating the base covariance matrix and deriving demand values. The findings demonstrate that this loop yields superior results compared to the standard Lasso method requiring direct transformation of continuous outputs into demand.

This study investigates a system of $N$ oscillators featuring nonlinear frequencies that depend on phase amplitudes, specifically focusing on cases where the nonlinear dependence is minimal. By assuming a weak nonlinear frequency dispersion and utilizing perturbation theory to derive approximate equations for a rescaled complex vector representing oscillator states, the analysis establishes conditions for the existence and stability of phase-locked states. The results demonstrate that weak nonlinear dispersion can destabilize certain stable phase-locked configurations. Perturbation analysis reveals two mechanisms for this destabilization: first, eigenvalues associated with phase-shifted states migrate across the imaginary axis into the right-half plane; second, unstable local modes emerge from within the imaginary axis. Particularly for the weak dispersion scenario, the authors provide a comprehensive classification of stable phase-locked states and illustrate how stability properties undergo abrupt, discontinuous changes as system parameters vary.

Lov\'{a}s and Wilson introduced a recursive process to uniformly and randomly generate spanning trees, but this hybrid method combines Pippenger's deterministic algorithm for complete bipartite matrices with a recursive step for general graphs. The authors present a new algorithm that applies to general graphs with $m$ edges and $n$ vertices in quasi-linear time, $O(\frac{m}{n}\log^2 m + \log^2 n)$, significantly faster than the original runtime of $O(m\log^2 n)$. By incorporating matrix completion in a more efficient manner, we achieve this improvement. Additionally, we develop a fully polynomial-time randomized approximation scheme for sampling edges in sparse subgraphs of any graph with probability proportional to the sum of edge weights, running in $O(\frac{m}{n}\log^2 m + \log^2 n)$ time.

This paper introduces the T-Music Dataset, the inaugural resource offering diverse musical examples explicitly paired with corresponding audio recordings. Each dataset sample includes multi-dimensional representations such as note events, pitch chroma, rhythm, key, form, timbre, and time. Our dataset was constructed by extracting digital audio tracks from over 30,000 songs sourced via the Spotify Web API and annotating them with structured musical elements derived automatically through music information retrieval techniques and probabilistically from music theory. The T-Music Dataset is intended to support unsupervised or semi-supervised cross-modal representation learning for both music and audio, specifically enabling tasks like cross-modal retrieval, joint embedding generation for multi-modal inputs, and dropout-based unsupervised semi-supervised training for self-supervised models.

Widely accessible and meticulously curated, yet containing extensive data, repositories such as Wikidata demand sophisticated tools for effective exploration. Traditional interfaces often restrict users to rigid, developer-defined navigation paths that fail to accommodate diverse interaction styles or support collaborative insights. To address this,odia is an interactive data system designed to facilitate co-dialogue in front of digital datasets. By integrating textual conversation with various visualization formats, Ontodia empowers users to tailor their exploration strategies and engage in collective data insights. Initial evaluations confirm the system's potential to deepen both individual comprehension and group discussions regarding complex datasets.

In this study, we examine the ground state solutions of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation featuring a negative nonlinearity exponent within the $L^2$-subcritical regime. Our primary contribution is demonstrating the orbital stability of a specific family of traveling black solitons, a property that guarantees stability for traveling dark solitons whose velocity is sufficiently high. Additionally, our work establishes a stability result for quasi-periodic waves exhibiting $1/\sqrt{t}$ asymptotic decay in time for equations supporting black solitons. This proof relies heavily on our analysis of the spectrum and norm of the associated linearized operator, along with an estimate limiting multiplicity of its eigenvalues.

We introduce "Guidance on the Go," an extensible framework that leverages multiple navigation strategies to enhance the performance of NLP-based machine reading comprehension tasks. To ensure rapid development and experimentation of these strategies, we have built "Lotse," an integrated library within PyTorch designed for their implementation. Our lotse-powered guidance systems, tested on the Microsoft Azure Document Question Answering dataset, demonstrate that even simple techniques, such as top-K cumulative probabilities, yield measurable improvements. Testing additional strategies confirms the effectiveness of this approach, and with only minor adjustments, these methods can be applied to various question answering tasks. The complete lotse-powered guidance code is accessible via our repository at https://github.com/lyzhang1997/guidance_on_the_go.

This study investigates how control coils influence the shape of nested flux surfaces within a long cylinder configured with endplates, focusing on scenarios where the cylinder's width-to-length ratio is moderate. In this setup, the unstressed aspect ratio of the flux surfaces matches that of the physical boundary. We demonstrate that control coils enhance both the allowable flexibility and maximum size (volume) of the resulting configurations. Specifically, a system utilizing just three coils achieves a state comparable to one requiring five coils; in instances without any control coils, the required flexibility or volume exceeds thresholds that become unattainable once the inclusion of control coils exceeds four coils. Furthermore, a theoretical model based on elliptic function properties accurately predicts the transition points where desired flexibility or volume limits are exceeded.

An innovative method for measuring temperature in reactors is introduced, leveraging the resonance frequency shift of protons as a function of temperature to establish a precise thermometric probe. This approach utilizes a miniature solenoid coil positioned within a fluid stream, operating as both a sensor and the instrument-suspended component to withstand high temperatures and pressures. Once the probe is in the field, the sensor outside determines the fluid temperature by reading the probe's magnetic resonance frequency. This system relies on a dedicated sensor, which is driven by the principle of nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR). Functioning as a contact-based method, it has been developed specifically for use in steam generators and heat exchangers, offering superior accuracy, stability, and ease of installation.

This study investigates lattice-boson models featuring an $N$-component mixture with interactions limited to nearest neighbors. We demonstrate that lattice condensates with periodic structures are stable for both the uniform $\lambda$ field and interaction scenarios involving two distinct coupling constants. The allowable lattice periods are strictly constrained by the number of species $N$, permitting only formations with periods of one or two. Furthermore, we derive necessary conditions defining the parameter space for stable condensates and confirm the coexistence of multiple stable states, or phase multiplicity, within the system.

Sunspots are magnetically intense regions on the solar surface that frequently show magnetic transients traveling across their boundaries. Previous studies have demonstrated that most of these features result from magnetic flux ejected by solar flares outside the spot, with speeds typically ranging from 1 to 10 km/s. In this study, we report the detection of magnetic transients moving at significantly higher velocities—reaching up to 30 km/s—as they cross an intense sunspot near the disk center. Utilizing simultaneous observations from the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope (photographs) and the Vector Solar Telescope (magnetograms), we determined that these fast-moving disturbances possess negative polarity and move opposite in direction to the spot's dominant magnetic field. Furthermore, DTSP (Doppler, Temperature, and Spectral Polarimetry) imaging reveals a narrow, intense channel of strong magnetic fields extending 1–2 spot radii from the spot's edge, where these filaments exhibit intense longitudinal magnetization oriented perpendicular to the filament's path and show positive Doppler shifts, indicating material outflows. These findings suggest a mechanism in which filaments of magnetic fields are stretched and thinned as filaments of opposite polarity grow from the spot's periphery, with the observed motion dictated by the MHD pinching effect.

This work examines a scaling investigation of the Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) preconditioner applied to second-order elliptic problems featuring heterogeneous coefficients. In BDDC, subdomains are balanced using a local weighted $l^2$-norm preconditioner, while constraints enforce boundary conditions through a global norm based on energy equivalent degrees of freedom. The study evaluates BDDC performance across four distinct preconditions, varying the local weighting scheme and selecting either one, two, or three equivalent degrees of freedom (EDFs) based on corner, edge, and all EDF types respectively. Results demonstrate that BDDC algorithmic performance is independent of the number of subdomains and the equivalent degrees of freedom included, relying solely on two key parameters: the chosen local EDF norms and the nature of the heterogeneous coefficients. Furthermore, numerical evidence indicates that preconditions incorporating all EDFs offer the strongest balance between precomputation overhead and iterative solver accuracy, rendering them the most effective for such problems.

Conventional analysis of user tagging systems primarily examines individual contributors in isolation. This study shifts focus to the collective dynamics of tags within an entire system, investigating the correlations between users and their activities. By analyzing these patterns, we aim to reveal insights into user behavior that inform the creation of novel tagging mechanisms and features. Specifically, we introduce a new approach for tag suggestion that leverages correlations among labels to enhance recommendations. We demonstrate that the relationships between different users' tagging behaviors, along with temporal patterns in their actions, can significantly enhance the precision of suggesting tags.

This study presents an analytical framework to assess how these effects influence the effective properties of three-dimensional porous porous permeable porous metamaterials composed of periodic polymeric foam. The framework adapts the Mualem-Dormy model, originally for air-water systems, to a single-fluid configuration, subsequently modified via volume averaging to derive an adjusted版本的 of Bruggeman model tailored for this scenario. Comparisons with commercial finite element simulations reveal that when based on a Bruggeman model, the inclusion of thermoviscous corrections is essential for accurately predicting the effective dynamic behavior of large-scale porous metamaterials.

Mobile Integrated Access and Backhaul (mIAB) enables user equipment (UE) moving in similar trajectories to share a single radio link, thereby improving spectral efficiency and reducing interference. However, determining the most effective set of users to pair requires balancing the gains in spectral efficiency against potential losses in access rate. This paper introduces a novel trajectory-based algorithm designed to maximize the system-wide cumulative access rate. By applying trajectory clustering, we initially identify representative trajectories and the associated subset of users for each cluster. Subsequently, an online algorithm dynamically allocates these trajectories to base stations using only current trajectory data, eliminating the need for full historical trajectory knowledge. Additionally, an optimized power control strategy further enhances cumulative access rates. Simulation results demonstrate that this proposed solution outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches.

Hyperparameters are essential components that must be configured to enable machine learning models to perform optimally. While prior research has established that specific hyperparameter choices lead to better algorithm performance, that same work often treats each parameter in isolation, overlooking how they might interact. This study investigates whether hyperparameters function independently or through mutual interactions, using a methodology designed to detect such effects. We analyze three classifiers—Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and Support Vector Machine—across combined datasets of size 200,000, evaluating each with 20 distinct configurations. Our analysis reveals that most feature and parameter interactions are negligible; however, we identify a specific, meaningful interaction between the Random Forest number of trees and the dataset's imbalance ratio. We also evaluate the consistency of these findings by testing them on two separate new datasets.

This study presents a classical derivation of spectral line energy quantization that parallels the spectral energy term by term with that of the electromagnetic field required for statistical equilibrium. Specifically, the spectral lines corresponding to the Balmer series in hydrogen are described as energy quantization intervals within the field, consistent with Planck's law of blackbody radiation. The proposed framework utilizes a model where spectral lines function both as discrete energy packets and as a mechanism for statistical equilibrium between them and the radiation field. A key component is the introduction of a new constant, the "quantum efficiency," which represents the probability that a specific line absorbs a quantum of energy from the radiation field. This quantum efficiency is determined by the oscillator strength of the spectral line. The work begins with a two-level system and extends to more complex configurations, offering insights into the nature of spectral lines and their interaction with radiation fields. Ultimately, the authors suggest that this classical reasoning may aid in formulating a more robust quantum theory of how atomic lines engage with electromagnetic fields.

We introduce a new curriculum for visual reasoning that is tailored to assess the reinforcement learning (RL) capability of navigating controlled curriculum changes. Situated within the Successor Feature framework, this approach automates the generation of successive tasks by employing a generative model of visual scenes coupled with a neural rule learner. By simating a "textbook" curriculum that adheres to a hierarchy of visual concepts and grammars, this method ensures task progressivity and provides consistent difficulty scaling. We demonstrate that this system automatically constructs a complex, yet structured, task sequence for the Neural Graphics Programming task that surpasses in difficulty the manually crafted benchmarks found in prior research. Additionally, our curriculum exposes agents to a broader spectrum of environments and significantly reduces the sample samples required for mastery compared to the non-structured random or manually designed curricula.

Liger serves as a robust Python framework designed for executing data-intensive computations within distributed environments, specifically leveraging Apache Spark and its extensions, including MLlib, graph processing, and SQL capabilities. It facilitates the integration of intricate research pipelines by providing automatic infrastructure for both debugging and live monitoring of data flows. This paper details the underlying data model and mechanisms that enable data sharing and movement within the system. Additionally, it examines two critical internal components: the Data Reduction System (DRS), which utilizes content-aware techniques to minimize data movement, and the comprehensive monitoring system used for tracing execution and data states. To demonstrate its efficacy, the authors describe two case studies involving large-scale image recognition and genomic analysis, underscoring ligers capacity to handle complex, multi-component pipelines effectively. Source code and documentation are hosted at http://liger.readthedocs.io/.

Recent research into novel methods for polarisation control via the geometric phase has generated significant enthusiasm within the scientific community, particularly for applications in spintronics and nonlinear optics. This paper offers a comprehensive review of present progress in geometric polarisation control within magnetic systems, presenting theoretical models alongside numerical simulations. We examine three distinct approaches: spin precession in a rotating frame, precession under a spatially periodic exchange field, and photon generation within a Kerr medium. Although these methods operate on different principles, each is examined for its potential practical utility and potential for future development in achieving geometric polarisation control.

We examine the weak noise limits of Kardar-Parisi-Zhang type equations, demonstrating both scenarios where solutions exist and where they do not, contingent upon comparing the parameter $\lambda$ against a specific critical size. Additionally, we establish upper and lower bounds regarding this critical threshold. These findings extend previous research by Deng and Zhang (2020), removing their requirement for the noise to be white. In our analysis of noise with a general, non-negative, integrable correlation function $f$, we employ novel techniques to represent solutions using random fields derived from heat kernel representations of noise. This approach enables stronger regularity assessments for the resulting solution random fields.

The COVID-19 pandemic has triggered a global public health crisis, prompting governments worldwide to implement restrictive measures aimed at slowing transmission. To evaluate the efficacy of these policies, authorities rely heavily on real-time infection data; however, such data is often absent, unreliable, or delayed. The challenge is particularly acute in low-resource nations like South Africa, where publicly accessible data is sparsely published and inconsistently formatted. This study investigates the quality of South African COVID-19 data by conducting a comprehensive analysis of all publications available on the country's official portal. By assessing the structural and semantic integrity of these documents, we identify specific shortcomings and deficits. Our findings suggest viable mitigation strategies, including automated monitoring systems for data quality that enable early warning alerts. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that data mining and quality assessment techniques are essential tools for enhancing data utility in times of crisis.

Multi-modal deep learning has become a pivotal area within computer vision, yet existing fusion techniques often fail to fully exploit the distinct advantages offered by different data sources. This study introduces a hierarchical fusion framework designed to combine image and graph representations effectively for person re-identification. Unlike early fusion methods, which merge inputs at the feature level and risk losing modal-specific characteristics, and unlike intermediate fusion approaches that require multiple fusion steps, our model employs a multi-scale hierarchical structure. This design allows for the integration of image and graph data at various stages, continuously balancing and leveraging the unique strengths of each modality. Empirical evaluations on the Reg3D and StBike datasets demonstrate the superiority of hierarchical fusion over both conventional strategies, confirming its enhanced capability in synthesizing distinct representation types.

We introduce a novel, unsupervised approach designed to analyze electronic health records (EHR) specifically for predicting the likelihood of ICU admission among patients with COVID-19. By leveraging clustering techniques and association rules, this method identifies distinctive patient features regarding ICU placement that are independent of any preconceived labels or categories. These discovered characteristics enable the precise tailoring of ICU resources to high-risk individuals, thereby optimizing the efficient use of these essential facilities. Crucially, because this technique necessitates no training on labeled data, it can be deployed immediately upon the collection of new, unseen EHR data.

This study examines the Schrödinger-like operator arising in a spherical ball within $\mathbb{R}^N$ under boundary conditions characterized by the nonlocal integral term $\int_{\Omega} |\nabla u|^2 d x$. Our primary goal is to investigate the asymptotic behavior of the resulting transmission eigenvalues and functions as the gradient constant $\theta$ and the parameter $\alpha$ increase. Our analysis demonstrates that for fixed values of $\theta$ and $\alpha$, transmission eigenfunctions exhibit a localized behavior in neighborhoods of the sphere's boundary. Furthermore, it is proven that as the gradient constant $\theta$ and parameter $\alpha$ grow larger, these eigenfunctions become increasingly localized near the sphere's surface. Additionally, numerical simulations were conducted to examine how varying $\theta$ and $\alpha$ influences the distribution and concentration of the eigenfunctions.

A universal bundle functor $P$ over the category of universal covers establishes a strong splitting of the associated monad in the category of simplicial groups. Conversely, any such strong splitting can be used to construct a corresponding universal bundle functor. These results generalize the findings of Bastin and Cegarra regarding universal covers of topological spaces.

We demonstrate that the logarithm of the subgroup count scales proportionally with the square root of the order of these symmetric and alternating groups. Additionally we show that the subgroup count for any specific root of the order of these symmetric and alternating groups converges to a lognormal distribution as the group size grows. We also derive a lower bound estimate for the number of subgroups within root-of-the-order collections of these symmetric and alternating groups.

Visual Relationship Detection (VRD) focuses on predicting relationships within an image based on a set of candidate proposals. These proposals, often generated by pre-trained object detectors, are heavily biased toward common classes and frequent inter-class associations, which hinders a model's ability to learn from rare instances. To address this imbalance, we introduce Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), a strategy designed to equalize the distribution of rare and frequent relationships in the training data. BNPS achieves this by proactively selecting negative relationship samples drawn from a pool of candidate negative proposals, specifically tailored to rare relations. Furthermore, we integrate the Balanced Sampling Loss (BSL) to optimize our approach, which re-weights positive and negative samples to prevent training dominance by the majority class. Experiments conducted on the Visual Relationship Dataset 2016 (VRD210C) demonstrate that combining BNPS with BSL yields significant performance gains over conventional training methods, particularly in accurately detecting rare relationships.

Drawing inspiration from the concept of quantum information extraction during unitary evolution via information scrambling, this study examines how residual quantum information within a many-body system can be harvested through local weak measurements. The approach involves applying a carefully tuned strong unitary operation following a delicate weak measurement. The results demonstrate that after a sufficient period, utilizing a specific class of optimal unitaries allows one to extract approximately maximal quantum information from the target system. Furthermore, the resulting post-measurement state approximates a maximally entangled pure state involving the measured system and another. Finally, the research investigates the dynamics of an incoherent quantum channel resulting from successive weak measurements interspersed with strong unitaries, revealing an interesting interplay between information scrambling and the preservation of quantum coherence.

Social relationships are pivotal to human existence, yet their dynamics remain difficult to quantify. This paper introduces a novel spatio-temporal graph neural network designed to forecast the evolution of social relations. By utilizing locations and check-in timestamps as graph features, the model represents social interactions as edges. We employ Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) to establish long-term dependencies across time, effectively refining the social graph through relationship state updates. Furthermore, a proposed location encoder and terrain graph mechanism incorporate geographical contexts into social structures. Our approach also leverages external data sources, including POI categories and road networks, to enhance social modeling. Empirical results demonstrate that this relationship prediction framework surpasses previous state-of-the-art methodologies.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) have become a focal point of research due to their capacity to model intricate relationships within data. However, the computational complexity of GNNs scales with the graph's size, rendering them impractical for large-scale applications. To address this, we introduce an end-to-end trainable method for the adaptive sampling of nodes in GNNs. This technique identifies and retains a small, representative subset of nodes while discarding the rest, thereby lowering computational costs. Crucially, we have developed a novel cross-entropy loss function that enables the learnable, joint optimization of the sampling process and the downstream task-specific network. Extensive experiments across multiple graph datasets and various classification tasks demonstrate that our approach not only significantly cuts computation time with minimal impact on performance but also yields superior results for classification compared to prior sampling techniques.

This paper introduces a novel methodology for implementing Multiple Constant Multiplication (MCM) circuits that propagates signal errors to minimize overall system mistake magnitude. Error awareness is integrated into the MCM flow by leveraging dedicated minimization algorithms and circuits designed with intrinsic mistake estimation capabilities. These capabilities enable a comparative analysis of alternative realizations to selectively choose the configuration with the smallest error at each circuit stage. The effectiveness of the proposed approach was validated through application to several case studies, demonstrating that when analog-to-digital converters possess a resolution of 12 bits or more, the suggested technique reduces the total system mistake by 25% to 50% compared to traditional techniques that ignore error impact.

While deep learning has transformed the landscape of machine learning over the past decade, research into its application on quantum computers lags far behind classical methods. This paper introduces a novel deep learning model based on a quantum neural network architecture designed to enhance classification tasks through the integration of multiple quantum circuit variants. We evaluate and compare different circuit models using both synthetic and real-world datasets. The results highlight a new approach combining several effective quantum circuits, which improves generalization and classification accuracy. We also analyze how dataset size and network hyperparameters influence performance. Finally, we discuss the practical hurdles and future avenues for quantum deep learning.

Over the past decade, advancements in radio frequency (RF) technology have enhanced the performance and expanded the application scope of accelerulators beyond high-energy physics, now benefiting fields such as nuclear physics, isotope production, and cancer therapy. This review examines recent RF innovations and their applications across these diverse areas. Key topics include an examination of novel pulse power technologies alongside a survey of various resonator designs. The paper explores methods for lowering RF power consumption, analyzing the benefits of single-cell and multi-cell geometries, the use of high-impedance slow-wave structures, and optimized coupling techniques. Additionally, the text addresses strategies for minimizing system heat load through advanced cooling, low heat-conduction materials, and improved thermal management designs. Finally, the effects of surface roughness on electron emission are explored, demonstrating how 3D simulation modeling aids in predicting and mitigating particle emission risks.

The muon collider is recognized as a highly valuable tool for investigating physics beyond the Standard Model. The project's complexity stems from its design and operational requirements, which heavily rely on managing the distinctive properties of the muon beam. To function effectively, a muon collider demands sophisticated components across the entire complex, including the accelerator, kicker systems, radio-frequency (RF) section, cryogenics infrastructure, and detector system. This paper offers a comprehensive overview of the muoid collider concept, examining its general layout, technical challenges, and the associated subsystems in detail.

We examine relativistic fluids with viscosity and theories exhibiting partial gauge symmetry, focusing on dispersion relations for scalar and vector modes. Findings indicate that, within this context, dispersion relations derived via various theoretical approaches—specifically using hydrodynamic gradient expansions up to second order in momentum—or those obtained through various forms of gauge-fixing remain mutually consistent. This conclusion holds regardless of whether dissipation is present.

We examine the semi-classical Hawking radiation emitted by primordial black holes (PBHs) within our current cosmological epoch. Unlike the standard thermally modeled emission, we derive exact formulas for PBH radiation in every channel, accounting specifically for Tipler-Price paradox. Our findings reveal that the peak of the Hawking spectrum shifts toward higher energies for lighter particles. Consequently, the emission rate of low-energy photons exhibits substantially elevated values compared to conventional thermal models. These elevated non-thermal rates imply that PBHs with masses around $10^{15}$ g would generate a significant local flux of low-energy photons. We propose that this enhanced emission could help explain the unaccounted-for component of the diffuse gamma-ray background observed at low energies.

This paper introduces a hardware implementation of a multi-threaded, single-machine probabilistic satisfiability solver designed for reliable circuit performance evaluation under noisy conditions. By leveraging a processor with a multi-pipelined architecture to accelerate parallel circuit assessments and utilizing multiple threads per process to enhance resource utilization, the system effectively mitigates noise while maintaining privacy through a modified probabilistic sampling algorithm. This approach eliminates the need for repetitive runs, enabling accurate and precise circuit evaluation in a single execution.

Natural language parsing involves predicting the syntactic structure of an input based on a set of annotated parse trees. While state-of-the-art neural parsers utilize vast amounts of training data, they are ill-equipped for low-resource scenarios where only a limited number of annotations are available. We introduce a novel framework, FPIO, designed to project parse trees from rich annotations onto inputs lacking them through cross-paragraph parsing. We demonstrate that FPIO significantly surpasses existing few-shot methods and even conventional parser models trained without syntax guidance, specifically by leveraging the inherent tree structure of training data to inform predictions using limited examples. Specifically, FPIO exceeds 90% exact match on TreeEdit distance for 10-parser few-shot natural language parsing tasks across four natural language processing domains using only ten annotated trees. The source code for FPIO can be accessed at: https://github.com/lyllylyl/FPIO.

This paper addresses semantic over-underwater image analysis using hyperspectral imagery. By leveraging the superior spectral resolution of these images, we refine the manual annotation lines to provide more accurate ground truth for training and assessing segmentation models. Additionally, a new dataset is introduced featuring 20 distinct underwater plant species. The study evaluates several segmentation techniques, comparing them to a proposed model based on a ResNet-101 backbone enhanced with a multi-task network architecture. Experimental results indicate that this model outperforms all existing methods on the new dataset.

This study presents the outcomes of a spectroscopic and photometric analysis of KIC 9267654, a G0V solar-type star identified by KIC data as exhibiting periodic, non-synchronous rotation. Our high-resolution spectra, gathered over four years, confirm these rotational modulations and quantify their polarities and equatorial speeds. Marked by a distinct inflection point near 40% of the stellar radius, the resulting rotation profile is atypical. We explore various mechanisms that could account for these anomalies, including magnetic activity, spots, or a stellar companion. Our findings indicate that neither magnetic activity nor a binary system adequately explain the observed behavior, leading us to hypothesize a stellar collision with a companion as the most likely cause.

We introduce an $i$-RAM model of computation that incorporates pointers to handle polynomials as integers efficiently. In this model, the distance between two polynomial addresses serves as a valid index for array access operations. We demonstrate the feasibility of performing bitwise operations and computations on polynomial integers within this framework. Specifically, we show how to implement fundamental operations—addition, multiplication, division, and modulo—as well as generating random numbers all in linear time complexity. We also prove the existence of a data structure capable of representing bit sets, enabling efficient set operations with quadratic time complexity relative to the number of elements. Furthermore, we establish a 2D grid data structure to support point storage and retrieval operations with at most logarithmic query time.

Self-supervised learning has emerged as a powerful technique for enhancing deep learning models, particularly in scenarios lacking extensive labeled datasets. Within session-based recommendation systems, data augmentation serves as a critical data enhancement strategy to improve system performance. This study introduces a novel approach leveraging self-supervised learning to optimize data augmentation specifically for these systems. By employing contrastive learning to establish meaningful relationships between subsequent sessions, we simultaneously augment dataset size and elevate sample quality. Additionally, this method effectively leverages unlabeled data often present in recommendation environments. Experimental results utilizing the Amazon datasets demonstrate that self-supervised data augmentation surpasses conventional techniques, yielding higher prediction accuracy.

This study introduces a novel construction of linear codes with a minimum weight equal to their dimension (LCD codes) via group rings. We demonstrate that constraints imposed on the selected group ring elements can significantly influence the characteristics of the generated LCD codes. Furthermore, we provide additional instances of these codes, drawn from the group rings of cyclic orders ranging from 3 to 9.
